en: The Bodhicaryāvatāra composed by Śāntideva. Om, homage to the Buddha!

Chapter One: The Praise of the Awakening Mind (Bodhicittānuśaṃsā) Having respectfully prostrated to all the Sugatas together with their Sons and their Dharma-bodies, as well as to all those worthy of veneration,
I shall explain, in brief and according to the scriptures, the entry into the vow of the Sons of the Sugatas.
Indeed, there is nothing new here to be said, nor do I possess any skill in composition;
for this very reason, I have no thought for the benefit of others—I have done this merely to cultivate my own mind.
First, by this means, the surge of my faith to cultivate virtue increases;
furthermore, if another person of a nature similar to mine should see it, then for that reason as well, this [practice] is purposeful.
This attainment of the favorable moment is extremely difficult to find; it is the means for accomplishing the goals of human life.
If one does not contemplate what is beneficial now, how will such an opportunity ever come together again?
Just as lightning momentarily reveals light in the dense darkness of night,
so too, through the power of the Buddhas, may the mind of the world occasionally turn toward merit for even a moment.
Therefore, virtue is always weak, whereas the power of evil is great and most terrible;
how could that evil be conquered by any other virtue if it were not for the mind of complete enlightenment?
The Lords of Sages, having reflected for many eons, have seen that this alone is beneficial;
for it is by means of happiness itself that happiness increases and carries across immeasurable multitudes of beings.
Those who wish to cross over the hundreds of sufferings of existence, those who wish to remove the misfortunes of sentient beings,
and those who wish to enjoy hundreds of manifold pleasures must never, indeed, let go of the mind of enlightenment.
The wretched one, bound by the prison of cyclic existence, is called a son of the Sugatas in an instant;
indeed, as soon as the thought of awakening has arisen, he becomes worthy of veneration by the world of humans and gods.

Having taken this image of impurity, one fashions from it an image of the jewel-like Victor, priceless and made of a substance exceedingly penetrating; seize firmly that which is known as the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).

O you who are habituated to wandering through the cities of the various realms of existence, take firm hold of the jewel of the spirit of enlightenment— a treasure thoroughly examined by those of immeasurable wisdom as being of great value, and the sole caravan leader for the world.
Like a plantain tree, everything else that is wholesome indeed perishes once its fruit has been abandoned;
however, the tree of the spirit of enlightenment (bodhicitta) constantly bears fruit and never undergoes exhaustion, but rather continues to produce more.
Since one can cross over even the most terrible sins in an instant by taking refuge in him—
just as one escapes great dangers by relying on a hero— how is it that ignorant beings do not take refuge in him?
It consumes great sins in an instant, like the fire at the end of an eon;
the wise Lord Maitreya proclaimed its immeasurable benefits to Sudhana.
That bodhicitta should be understood, in brief, as being of two kinds:
the mind of aspiration for enlightenment and the mind of engagement in enlightenment.
Just as a distinction is perceived between one who desires to go and one who is actually going,
so too should the distinction between these two be understood by the wise according to their respective order.
The mind of the vow for enlightenment yields great fruit even within saṃsāra;
however, it does not possess the quality of uninterrupted merit in the same way as the mind of application.
From the moment one resolves with an irreversible mind to liberate the infinite realm of sentient beings, [one becomes a bodhisattva].
From that time forward, even while one is asleep or heedless,
uninterrupted streams of merit flow forth like the sky, manifold times over.
The Tathāgata himself stated this, along with its logical justification, in the *Subāhupṛcchā*, for the sake of beings who have inferior inclinations. (SBca 1.20)
Thinking, "I shall destroy the headaches of sentient beings," one who possesses a beneficial intention is embraced by immeasurable merit.
How much more so for one who desires to remove the incomparable spear of each [being],
and who wishes to establish each being as a possessor of immeasurable virtues?
For whose mother or father could such a wish for their welfare exist?
Or will it belong to the deities, the sages, or the Brahmas?
Even for those very same beings, such a desire for their own sake has never arisen before, even in a dream; how then could it possibly arise for the sake of others?
How can this unprecedented and extraordinary jewel of a being be born, whose intention for the sake of others does not arise even for its own self? (SBca 1.25)
How indeed can the merit of the jewel of the mind— the seed of the world’s bliss and the medicine for the world’s suffering— be measured?
The worship of the Buddha is distinguished even by the mere wish for their welfare;
how much more so when one exerts oneself for the sake of the complete happiness of all sentient beings!
Driven by the desire for escape from suffering, they rush headlong into suffering itself;
out of delusion and a craving for happiness, they destroy their own well-being like an enemy.
Whoever would bring satisfaction with all forms of happiness to those who are repeatedly afflicted by the theater of suffering, and who would cut through all their afflictions; SBca_1.29.
He even destroys delusion; how could anyone be equal to such a virtuous person?
Where is there such a friend, or where is there such merit?
Even one who returns a favor for a service received is praised;
how much more so, then, a Bodhisattva who acts as a benefactor without being solicited?

One who provides a sacrificial feast for a few people is honored by others as a doer of merit simply because they give food for a single moment, whereas one who sustains others for half a day is treated with contempt. (SBca 1.32)
How much more so for one who, throughout limitless time, bestows upon an infinite number of sentient beings—
indestructible as long as the world and its inhabitants endure— the complete fulfillment of every desire?
Thus, the Lord has said that whoever harbors impurity within their own heart toward the Son of the Conqueror,
the master of the sacrificial session, shall dwell in the hells for as many eons as there are particles of that arising impurity.
Now, for one whose mind attains serenity, from that [serenity] a greater fruit shall arise;
for evil toward the Sons of the Conquerors is produced by great effort, whereas virtue arises without exertion.
I pay homage to their bodies, in whom that precious jewel of the supreme mind has arisen;
I go for refuge to those mines of happiness, in whom even an injury results in a succession of bliss.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Benefits of the Awakening Mind," in the *Pañjikā* on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
Chapter Two: Confession of Sin.

In order to grasp that jewel of the mind, I now perform perfect worship of the Tathāgatas, of the stainless jewel of the True Dharma, and of the sons of the Buddha, who are oceans of virtue. (SBca 2.1)
As many flowers and fruits as there are, and whatever kinds of medicinal plants exist;
as many jewels as there are in the world, and waters that are clear and delightful.
There are mountains made of jewels, as well as other forest regions delightful for their solitude,
with creepers radiant with the ornaments of flowers, and trees whose branches are bowed down by excellent fruit.
And in the worlds of the gods and others, there are perfumes and incenses, wish-fulfilling trees, and trees made of jewels;
as well as lakes adorned with lotuses and the utterly enchanting calls of swans.
And all these various kinds of crops grown without cultivation, or other objects of worship and adornment,
extending as far as the limits of the expanse of space— all these are without ownership.
Having taken this with my intellect, I offer it to the preeminent sages together with their sons;
may they, who are most worthy of offerings and great compassion, accept it from me out of pity for me.
I am devoid of merit and greatly impoverished; I have nothing else for the purpose of worship.
Therefore, O Protectors whose minds are intent on the welfare of others, please accept this for my sake through your own power.
I give myself entirely and in every way to the Victors and likewise to their sons; O Supreme Beings, accept me as your own, for out of devotion I enter into the state of servitude to you.
Through being taken into your care, O Lord, I shall be fearless and work for the welfare of sentient beings in existence;
I shall transcend my former evil and shall not commit further sin again.
In those fragrant bathing halls, delightful with pillars radiant with jewels and canopies shimmering with pearls, where the crystal floors are clear, bright, and expansive.
With many jars made of great jewels, filled with pleasingly fragrant water and flowers,
I perform this bath for the Tathāgatas and their sons, accompanied by song and instrumental music.
I wipe their bodies with incomparable garments that have been well-washed, perfumed, and cleansed of stains;
thereafter, I give them excellent robes that are beautifully dyed and well-perfumed.
With divine garments that are soft, smooth, and variegated in beauty, and with various excellent ornaments,
I shall adorn Samantabhadra, Ajita, Mañjughoṣa, Lokeśvara, and the others as well.

I anoint the bodies of all the lords of sages, which blaze with the luster of gold that is well-heated, polished, and well-washed, with the finest perfumes whose scents spread throughout the entire triple-thousandfold world system.
Worship the most worshipful lords of sages with all fragrant and delightful flowers, such as the māndārava, indīvara, and mallikā, and with garlands that are beautiful in their arrangement.
I incense them with clouds of incense, delightful with their abundant and shimmering fragrance;
and I offer to them various kinds of foods to be eaten, chewed, and drunk as a presentation.
I offer rows of jewel-lamps set within golden lotuses,
and upon floors anointed with fragrance, I scatter pleasing heaps of flowers.

I offer to those whose nature is loving-kindness clouds of celestial palaces, which are radiant, beautifying the faces of the directions, adorned with long, dangling strings of pearls and gems, and made delightful by songs of praise.
I shall hold aloft the most beautiful jeweled parasols of the great sages— exquisitely formed with golden handles and adorned with closely set pearls.
From this point forward, let delightful clouds of worship arise,
as well as clouds of musical instruments and songs that bring joy to all sentient beings.
And upon all the jewels of the true Dharma, upon stupas, and upon images,
may showers of flowers, jewels, and the like fall continuously.
Just as Mañjughoṣa and the others worship the Victors,
so do I worship the Tathāgatas, the Protectors, together with their Sons.
I praise those oceans of virtue with hymns that are like oceans of melodic notes;
may clouds of musical praise arise from these without fail.
With prostrations as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields, I bow down to all the Buddhas of the three times, together with their supreme assemblies of Dharma.
I pay homage to all caityas, as well as those that are the abodes of Bodhisattvas;
I offer salutations to my preceptors and likewise to the ascetics who are worthy of reverence.
I go for refuge to the Buddha until I reach the seat of enlightenment;
I go for refuge to the Dharma and likewise to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
With palms joined in reverence, I make this request to the Perfectly Awakened Ones who reside in all directions, and also to the Bodhisattvas who possess great compassion.
In this beginningless saṃsāra, or even in this very life,
whatever sin has been committed or caused to be committed by me, who am like a beast;
And whatever I have rejoiced in for the sake of my own destruction out of delusion— that transgression I confess, tormented by remorse.
Whatever harm I have done to the Three Jewels, or to my mother and father,
or to other gurus and others, through the impulsive actions of body, speech, and mind;
O Leaders, whatever terrible sin has been committed by me, a wicked person defiled by manifold faults, all of that I now confess.
And how may I escape from this? O Leaders, I am constantly filled with anxiety;
may death not come upon me before my accumulation of evil has been exhausted.
And how may I escape from this? Save me quickly!
Lest death should come swiftly upon me while my sins remain unexhausted.
This death, which destroys one's trust, does not examine what has been done or left undone;
it is untrustworthy to both the healthy and the sick, like a sudden, great thunderbolt.
"Because of the causes of the pleasant and the unpleasant, many kinds of evil have been committed;
that one must depart, leaving everything behind—this was not understood. (SBca 2.35)
Those who are unpleasant will not exist; those who are dear to me will not exist;
I myself will not exist, and everything will not exist.
Whatever object is experienced becomes an object of memory;
like everything experienced in a dream, once it has passed, it is no longer seen.
While you remain right here, many loved ones and those not loved have already passed away;
yet the terrible evil committed for their sake remains standing before you.
Thus, I did not reflect that "I am a stranger," and through delusion, attachment, and aversion, I have committed manifold evils.
Day and night, without ceasing, the expenditure of life increases;
yet there is no further arrival of life—how then can I think, "I shall not die"?
Even here, while lying on my bed and surrounded by kinsmen,
I must endure the agonizing pain of the severing of my vital organs and other such sufferings all alone.
When one is seized by the messengers of Yama, where is the kinsman? Where is the friend? At that time, merit alone is protection; yet that was not cultivated by me.
O Protectors, through attachment to this impermanent life and by failing to recognize this danger,
I, being heedless, have accumulated much evil.
Even if led today for the purpose of having one's limbs severed, one becomes parched;
thirsty and with a wretched gaze, one perceives the world as something entirely different.
How much more so when one is presided over by the messengers of Yama in their terrifying forms,
seized by the fever of great terror, and overcome by the discharge of excrement?
With terrified glances, seeking protection in the four directions, [he thinks]:
"Who will be a virtuous protector for me from this great fear?"
Seeing all directions devoid of protection, I shall again fall into utter confusion;
what then shall I do in that place of great terror?
This very day, I go for refuge to the Jinas, the lords of the world, who possess great power,
who are intent upon protecting the world, and who remove all fear.
And likewise, with my whole being, I go for refuge to the host of Bodhisattvas, who have realized the Dharma that destroys the fear of cyclic existence.
Overwhelmed by fear, I offer myself to Samantabhadra;
and once again, I offer myself to Mañjughoṣa by means of my own self.
And to that Lord Avalokita, whose conduct is agitated by compassion, I cry out with a wail of distress, terrified; may he protect me, a sinner.
Seeking protection, I call out with sincerity to the noble Ākāśagarbha and Kṣitigarbha, and to all those who possess great compassion.
I bow down to that Vajrī, at the mere sight of whom the wicked messengers of Yama and others flee in terror in the four directions.
Having transgressed your word, I now seek refuge in you out of fear; being terrified, quickly destroy my fear!
Even one who fears a minor illness should not disregard the physician's instructions;
how much more so when seized by the four hundred and four types of diseases?
For by even a single [fault], all the people dwelling in Jambudvīpa perish—
those for whom no remedy is to be found in any direction.
"In this matter, to think 'I shall transgress the word of the omniscient physician who removes all thorns'—fie upon me, utterly deluded! (SBca 2.57)
I remain exceedingly vigilant even regarding other precipices;
how much more so, then, regarding this precipice of many thousands of leagues that lasts for a long time?
Death does not come today alone; therefore, it is not fitting for me to dwell in ease.
That moment will inevitably arrive when I shall no longer exist.
"By whom has fearlessness been granted to me? How shall I escape?
I shall certainly cease to exist; why then is my mind so well-composed?"
What essence remains for me from those things previously experienced and now lost,
through my attachment to which I have transgressed the words of my gurus?
Having abandoned this world of the living, as well as my kinsmen and acquaintances, I shall go somewhere all alone; what use have I for all these things, pleasant or unpleasant?
At that time, this alone was my appropriate reflection day and night:
"Since suffering is certain to arise from the unwholesome, how might I escape from it?"
Whatever sin has been accumulated by me, foolish and deluded— whether it be naturally reprehensible or reprehensible by convention— [I confess it all].
Standing before the Protectors with palms joined, terrified by suffering, I confess all of that, prostrating again and again.
May the Leaders accept this transgression as a transgression;
O Protectors, this was not good, and it shall not be done by me again.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Confession of Evil," in the *Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā* composed by Prajñākaramati.

Chapter Three: The Embracing of the Awakening Mind (Bodhicitta) I rejoice with great joy in all the merit performed by all sentient beings, which provides rest from the sufferings of the miserable realms. May those who are suffering abide in happiness. (SBca 3.1)
I rejoice in the liberation of embodied beings from the suffering of saṃsāra;
and I rejoice in the state of a bodhisattva and the state of buddhahood of the Protectors.
And I rejoice in the oceans of the generation of the mind of enlightenment of the Teachers, which bring happiness to all sentient beings and establish the welfare of all sentient beings.
With palms joined in reverence, I entreat all the perfectly awakened ones in every direction:
may they kindle the lamp of Dharma for those who fall into suffering through delusion.
With palms joined in reverence, I entreat the Victors who desire to enter nirvāṇa:
may they remain for infinite eons, so that this world does not become blind.
Having thus performed all this, by whatever merit I have acquired,
may I become the pacifier of all the sufferings of all sentient beings.
May I become medicine for the sick, and likewise a physician and their attendant, until disease never arises again.
May I dispel the suffering of hunger and thirst by raining down food and drink;
during the intermediate kalpas of famine, may I become food and drink myself.
May I become an inexhaustible treasure for sentient beings who are poor,
and may I stand before them in the form of various useful articles.
I relinquish my very self, as well as enjoyments and all merit belonging to the three times, without attachment, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.
Nirvana consists in the relinquishing of everything, and my mind seeks nirvana;
if I must relinquish all things, let it rather be given to sentient beings.
Since I have made myself an object of misery for all embodied beings,
let them always strike me, revile me, or cover me with dust.
Let them play with my body, laugh, and sport;
I have given my body to them, so why should I worry about this?
And let them perform whatever actions bring them happiness;
may no misfortune ever befall anyone by taking me as their object.
For those whose minds become either angry or pleased by taking me as their object,
that very state shall be the cause for the perpetual accomplishment of all their aims.
Those who slander me, as well as others who do me harm, and even those who mock me—
all of them shall become partakers of enlightenment.
I am the protector of the protectorless, the caravan leader for those traveling the road, and for those desiring to reach the further shore, I am the boat, the bridge, and the causeway.
May I be a lamp for those seeking a lamp, a bed for those seeking a bed,
and a servant for all embodied beings who seek a servant.
May I become for embodied beings a wish-fulfilling gem, a jar of fortune, a perfected spell, a great medicinal herb, a wish-granting tree, and a cow of plenty.
The elements, such as earth and the rest, serve as various kinds of enjoyments for immeasurable beings dwelling throughout the entirety of space.
Thus, for the realm of sentient beings who abide in space,
may I be their source of sustenance in manifold ways until all have attained nirvāṇa.
Just as the Bodhicitta was previously taken up by the Sugatas of old, and just as they remained in the successive stages of the Bodhisattva training; SBca_3.22 //
In that same way, I generate this bodhicitta for the welfare of the world;
and in that very same way, I shall train in those precepts in their proper sequence.
Having thus grasped the thought of awakening with serene confidence,
the wise one should further gladden the mind in this way for the sake of strengthening it when questioned again.
Today my birth has become fruitful; a human existence has been well-attained.
Today I am born into the family of the Buddha; I am now truly a son of the Buddha.
Therefore, I must now act in such a way that no stain shall fall upon this stainless lineage of those who perform what is appropriate for their own family.
Just as a blind man might find a jewel among heaps of refuse,
so too has this bodhicitta somehow arisen within me.
This elixir has arisen for the destruction of the world's death;
it is an inexhaustible treasure that pacifies the world's poverty.
This is the supreme medicine that pacifies the diseases of the world;
it is the tree of rest for the world weary from wandering on the path of existence.
The moon of the mind has arisen as a common bridge for all travelers to cross over the miserable realms, and as a pacifier of the afflictions of the world.
It is the great sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance in the world;
it has arisen as the fresh butter produced from churning the milk of the sublime Dharma.
For this caravan of people traveling on the path of existence, who are hungry for the enjoyment of happiness,
this feast of bliss has indeed arrived, providing satisfaction to all sentient beings who have come as guests.
Today I have invited the world to the state of a Sugata and to happiness in the interim;
indeed, before all the Protectors, may the gods, asuras, and others rejoice!
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Adoption of the Awakening Mind," in the *Pañjikā* on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
Chapter Four: Heedfulness Regarding the Awakening Mind.
Having thus firmly grasped the awakening mind, the son of the Conquerors should always strive, without indolence, not to transgress the training. *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 4.1.
Even regarding that which was undertaken impulsively or that which was not properly deliberated upon, it is appropriate to make a vow, thinking, "I shall do this, or perhaps not. (SBca 4.2)
That which has been investigated by the Buddhas and their sons of great wisdom—
why should I not rely upon that very thing according to my own ability?
And if, having made such a vow, I were not to accomplish it through action,
what would be my destiny after deceiving all these beings?
It is said that even for a person who, having merely thought of giving in their mind, does not actually give— even regarding an object of very little value— they become a preta.
What will become of my destiny if, having loudly proclaimed with sincere devotion the unsurpassed bliss, I have deceived the entire world?
Only the Omniscient One knows this inconceivable course of karma,
whereby even when one abandons the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), he nonetheless liberates those people in such a manner.
For a bodhisattva, every transgression is thus extremely grave,
because by committing it, he causes the ruin of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, whoever else shall create even a moment's obstacle to his merit—
that destroyer of the welfare of sentient beings will have no end to his miserable rebirths.
For by destroying the welfare of even a single sentient being, one is destroyed;
how much more so for all embodied beings dwelling throughout the entirety of space?
Thus, wavering in saṃsāra due to the power of transgressions and the power of the spirit of enlightenment, one is delayed in attaining the [bodhisattva] stages.
Therefore, I must respectfully accomplish what I have vowed;
if I do not exert effort today, I shall go from the surface [of the earth] to the very depths below.
Immeasurable Buddhas, who seek the welfare of all sentient beings, have passed away;
yet because of my own faults, I have not come within the range of their healing power.
If even now I were to remain just as I am, I would repeatedly encounter the miseries of the lower realms, as well as disease, death, cutting, and dismemberment.
When shall I obtain the arising of a Tathāgata, faith, and human birth itself, as well as the fitness for the practice of virtue— all of which are so exceedingly difficult to find?
This day is healthy and free from calamity, accompanied by food;
yet this moment of life is deceptive, like a bubble formed upon water.
For by conduct such as mine, human birth will not be obtained again;
when human birth is not obtained, how can there be virtue, since only evil prevails?
When, though worthy of virtue, I do not practice it,
being deluded by the sufferings of the miserable realms, what shall I do then?
For one who performs no wholesome deed and instead accumulates evil,
even the very word "good rebirth" is lost for hundreds of millions of eons.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Human birth is extremely difficult to obtain, comparable to a turtle inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke in the great ocean. (SBca 4.20)
For a single moment’s committed sin, one dwells in Avīci for an eon;
what need is there to speak of the happy realms when one has accumulated sins since beginningless time?
Nor is he liberated merely by experiencing that [suffering];
therefore, even while experiencing it, he produces other evil.
There is no greater deception than this, nor any greater delusion,
that having obtained such a moment as this, I have not practiced what is wholesome.
If, however, I reflect thus and again sink down, deluded,
I shall grieve for a long time once more, driven by the messengers of Yama.
The unbearable fire of hell will burn my body for a long time;
but the fire of remorse will burn my untrained mind for a long time.
Having somehow reached this extremely rare ground of benefit,
even though I know it, shall I be led back once again to those very same hells?
In this matter, I have no volition, as if deluded by spells;
I do not know by whom I am bewildered, nor who dwells within me.
The enemies of craving, hatred, and so forth lack hands, feet, and other limbs;
they are neither brave nor wise. How then have I been enslaved by them?
Remaining right within my own mind and well-established there, they strike me down;
yet even then I do not become angry—fie upon this endurance of what is improper!
Even if all the gods and humans were my enemies,
they would not be capable of producing the fire of the Avīci hell.
When even the ashes of Mount Meru cannot be found due to its attachment [to the fire],
there the powerful enemies that are the afflictions cast me down in an instant.
For indeed, even the very long lifespans of all other enemies do not equal such a duration as that of my enemies,
the afflictions, which is immensely long and without beginning or end.
When cultivated in accordance with their nature, all things conduce to benefit;
yet these afflictions, when indulged in, produce nothing but extreme suffering.
Thus, while these constant and long-standing enemies— the sole cause for the production of a flood of calamities—
dwell within my heart, how could I possibly find joy in cyclic existence without fear?
These guardians of the prison of existence are also executioners who slay within the hells and other realms;
if they dwell in the chamber of my intellect within the cage of greed, how can there be happiness for me?
Therefore, I shall not lay down my burden here until these enemies have been slain before my eyes;
for even when the wrongdoer is insignificant, those who are exalted by pride and firmly bound by their wrath do not go to sleep without having destroyed him.

Fierce in their resolve at the forefront of battle, they do not turn back until they have achieved their goal, disregarding the pain of wounds from arrows and spears as they violently strike down the darkness of those suffering from natural death.

How much less, then, could there be any despondency or dejection in me today, even due to hundreds of calamities, for one who is intent on destroying the natural enemies—the constant causes of all suffering? For what reason indeed would such weakness arise?
Without any cause whatsoever, they carry the wounds inflicted by enemies upon their bodies like ornaments;
why then should sufferings be an obstacle for me, who am striving for the attainment of the great goal?

Fishermen, outcasts, farmers, and others whose minds are fixed solely upon their own livelihood endure the hardships of cold, heat, and so forth; why then should I not endure them for the sake of the welfare of the world?
Having made a vow to liberate the world, as far as the limits of space in the ten directions, from its afflictions,
even my own self has not been liberated from those very afflictions.
Speaking thus without knowing the measure of one's own strength is like the behavior of a madman;
therefore, I shall remain steadfast and never turn back in my constant effort to destroy the afflictions.
In this regard, I shall become a grasper, harboring enmity and engaging in conflict—
unless it be toward such afflictions that are inherently linked to the destruction of afflictions.
Let my entrails gush out at will, and let my head indeed fall;
yet I shall never, under any circumstances, bow down before the enemies that are the afflictions.

Even for an enemy who has been banished, there may still be the acquisition of a dwelling place in another land; however, such is not the case for the enemy of the afflictions, for once he has departed, he does not return with his power restored.
Where could that [enemy] go, dwelling within my own mind, having been cast out, yet remaining there striving for my destruction?
O dull-witted one, this is not merely my own effort; these wretched afflictions are to be overcome by wisdom and right view.
The afflictions do not reside in sense objects, nor in the collection of faculties, nor in the interval between them;
they do not exist elsewhere than these. Where, then, do they abide that they churn the entire world?
This is merely an illusion; therefore, release the fear from your heart and apply yourself to effort.
For the sake of wisdom, why do you needlessly torment yourself in the hells?
Having thus resolved, I shall exert effort for the sake of practicing the training as it has been taught;
for how can one who deviates from a physician’s instruction achieve freedom from disease when the illness is curable by medicine?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on Heedfulness regarding the Awakening Mind, in the *Pañjikā* (Detailed Commentary) on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
Chapter Five: Guarding Vigilant Awareness (Saṃprajanya) One who wishes to guard the training must guard the mind with effort;
for it is impossible to guard the training without guarding the flickering mind. (SBca 5.1)
Untamed rutting elephants do not cause such torment here as the elephant of the mind does when it is unleashed in the Avīci hell and other realms.
If the elephant of the mind is bound on all sides with the rope of mindfulness,
all fear has vanished and every excellence has arrived.
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, snakes, and all enemies;
all the guardians of hell, as well as ḍākinīs and rākṣasas.
All these become bound through the binding of the single mind;
and all become tamed through the taming of the single mind.
For it has been stated by the Speaker of Reality that all fears and immeasurable sufferings arise from the mind alone.
By whom were the weapons in hell diligently fashioned?
By whom was the floor of glowing iron made, and from where did those women arise?
The Sage declared that all those [sufferings] arise from an evil mind;
therefore, there is nothing more terrifying in the three worlds than the mind.
If the perfection of generosity consisted in making the world free from poverty,
then how could that have been achieved by the Protectors of the past, since the world is still poor today?
When there arises in all people the thought of relinquishing one's entire possession together with its fruit, that is called the perfection of generosity; therefore, it is indeed that thought itself.
Where could fish and other creatures be taken so that I would not kill them?
When the mind of renunciation is attained, however, that is considered the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
How many wicked people, who are like the sky, could I possibly kill?
For when the mind of anger is killed, all enemies are slain.
Where would there be enough leather to cover the entire earth?
Yet with a mere piece of leather for sandals, the whole world is covered.
In the same way, external objects cannot be warded off by me;
I shall restrain my own mind—what is the use of warding off anything else?
Even with both speech and body, that fruit does not arise for one of dull conduct;
whereas for even a single sharp mind, there is the state of Brahman and so forth.
The All-Knowing One has declared that all recitations and ascetic practices, even those performed over a long period of time, are in vain if performed with a distracted or dull mind.
Those who have not cultivated this secret mind, which is the very essence of all Dharma, wander in vain through the sky to destroy suffering and attain happiness. (SBca 5.17)
Therefore, I must keep my own mind well-established and well-guarded;
apart from the vow of guarding the mind, what is the use of many other vows for me? (SBca 5.18)
Just as one situated among the fickle protects a wound with care,
so too should one situated among the wicked always protect the wound of the mind.
Fearing even a tiny fraction of the pain from a physical wound, I protect that wound with great care;
why then do I not likewise protect the wound of the mind from being struck by the mountain-like aggregates?
For by dwelling in this state of mind, even among the wicked or in the midst of women, the steadfast ascetic is not corrupted.
Let my gains perish at will; let honor, body, and life perish; let everything else that is wholesome perish as well, but never, never my mind.
I join my palms in reverence to those who wish to protect the mind;
guard mindfulness and situational awareness with every effort.
Just as a man overwhelmed by disease is incapable of all activities,
so too a mind impaired by these two is incapable of all activities.
For one whose mind lacks clear awareness, that which has been heard, reflected upon,
and cultivated does not remain in memory, like water in a leaking jar.
Even many who are learned, faithful,
and diligent may become defiled by transgressions due to the fault of lack of introspection.
Even if they have accumulated merits, those who are robbed by the thief of non-introspection— which follows upon the theft of mindfulness— go to an evil rebirth.
This host of thieves that are the afflictions seeks an opportunity for entry;
once it has found an opening, it robs and destroys the life of the good rebirths.
Therefore, mindfulness should never be allowed to depart through the door of the mind;
even if it has gone away, it should be brought back by recollecting the agony of the miserable realms.
For those fortunate ones who show respect even out of fear of their preceptor’s instruction,
mindfulness arises easily through living with their teacher.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess unimpeded vision everywhere;
everything is before them, and I stand before them.
Having reflected thus, one should remain in that state, endowed with shame, reverence, and fear;
in this way, the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) will arise for him again and again.
When mindfulness stands guard at the gateway of the mind for the sake of protection, clear comprehension then arises and does not depart once it has arrived. (SBca 5.33)
First of all, this mind must be constantly established in such a way that I should always remain like a piece of wood, as if devoid of sense faculties.
One should never cast about the eyes fruitlessly;
rather, the gaze should always be directed downward, as if constantly looking inward.
However, for the sake of resting the gaze, one may occasionally look toward the directions;
and having seen a mere appearance, one should look back as a sign of welcome.
At the beginning of the path and so forth, one should repeatedly look in the four directions to become aware of danger;
having rested, one should look about the quarters and turn back to look behind.
Whether advancing or retreating, having first scrutinized what lies before and behind,
one should act after having thus understood the task at hand in all circumstances.
Having thus enjoined the action with the thought, "The body must be maintained in this way," one should again observe in the interval: "How is the body positioned? (SBca 5.39)
One should exert every effort to restrain the wild elephant of the mind,
so that once it is bound to the great pillar of reflection on the Dharma, it is not released.
One should thus examine the mind, asking "Where does it abide?",
so that one never abandons the yoke of meditative concentration for even a single moment.
If one is unable [to maintain discipline] due to circumstances such as fear or festivities, one may act according to one's ease;
for it has been stated that equanimity toward the precepts is permissible at the time of giving.
Having understood what one has begun to do, one should not think of anything else;
that very task should first be accomplished with an inner self absorbed in it.
For in this way all that is well-done is accomplished; otherwise, neither would come to pass.
Furthermore, the affliction of lack of clear comprehension will likewise continue to increase.
While various kinds of idle chatter occur in many ways and amidst all manner of curiosities, one should strike down the curiosity that has arisen.
If one should happen upon fruitless actions such as trampling clay, cutting grass, or drawing lines,
one should remember the training of the Tathāgata and, being afraid, abandon that very moment.
When one wishes to move or even wishes to speak,
one should first examine one's own mind and then act with fortitude and reason.
When one perceives that one's own mind is either attracted or repelled,
then one should neither act nor speak, but remain like a piece of wood.
When the mind becomes agitated or mocking, filled with pride and intoxication, excessively sarcastic, crooked, and deceitful; SBca_5.49 //
Whenever there arises the semblance of self-exaltation, or the disparagement of others,
accompanied by reproach and agitation, one should then remain as motionless as a log of wood.
If my mind seeks gain, honor, or fame, or again, seeks a retinue, or seeks service for myself, then I shall remain like a log of wood.
My mind desires to speak either what is harsh to others' interests, or what seeks its own self-interest, or simply out of a desire for an audience; therefore, I remain like a log of wood.
Because [others] are impatient, lazy, fearful, arrogant, talkative,
and likewise stubbornly attached to their own side, I therefore remain like a log of wood.
Thus, observing that the mind is either afflicted or engaged in fruitless undertakings,
the hero should always firmly restrain it by means of its antidote.
It should be well-ascertained, very serene, steadfast, respectful and reverent,
modest, apprehensive, peaceful, and intent upon the service of others.
Unwearied by the mutually contradictory desires of children, he is filled with compassion, thinking: "For this [suffering] arises from their afflictions; it is indeed theirs."
I shall always maintain my mind under the control of myself and sentient beings regarding blameless things, remaining free from pride like a magical creation.
Recalling again and again this excellent opportunity obtained after a long time,
I shall maintain such a mind as unshakable as Mount Sumeru.
Dragged here and there by vultures greedy for flesh, why does this body not act otherwise— why does it offer no resistance in this matter?
Why do you protect this mind, having made it your own by means of this physical body?
If this [body] is indeed distinct from you, then what loss to you is there in its destruction?
O fool, you do not accept a wooden puppet as pure;
why then do you protect this putrid machine constructed from impurities?
First, separate this skin-sack by means of your own intellect;
with the sword of wisdom, strip the flesh away from the skeleton.
Having even separated the bones, look at the marrow within;
consider for yourself whether there is any essence here.
Having thus searched with effort, you have not seen any essence here;
tell me now, why do you still protect this body?
You must not eat impurity, nor drink blood, nor suck on intestines; what will you do with this body?
It is appropriate to protect [the body] for the sake of food by vultures, jackals, and the like;
however, this little human body is merely an instrument for [one's] karma.
Even as you protect it in this way, merciless Death will snatch it away and deliver the body to the vultures; what then will you do?
One does not give clothing and other goods to a servant with the thought that he will remain [forever];
since the body will depart after having consumed [your resources], why do you incur such expense?
Having given him his wages from that [work], now direct your mind toward your own welfare;
for not everything acquired by a wage-earner is returned to him.
Having conceived the notion of a boat regarding the body, as it is the support for coming and going,
make the body move according to your will for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
Thus, having brought oneself under control, one should always have a smiling face;
one should abandon the contraction of the brow into a frown, being the first to speak and a friend to the world.
One should not suddenly throw down chairs and the like with a loud thud;
one should not bang doors, for one should always delight in silence.
The owl, the cat, and the thief, moving silently and with great caution, achieve their desired ends; in this same manner, the ascetic should always conduct himself.
One should always receive with one's head the words of those who are skilled in exhorting others and who provide unbidden assistance; one should always be a disciple to all.
One should utter words of approval for all well-spoken words;
and upon seeing one who performs meritorious deeds, one should gladden them with praises.
One should speak of virtues in one's absence and repeat them when others do so out of affection;
and when one's own qualities are being praised, one should cultivate the recognition of those virtues as belonging to others.
For all undertakings are for the sake of satisfaction, yet that is difficult to obtain even with riches;
therefore, I shall enjoy the happiness of contentment through qualities produced by the labor of others.
In this case, there is no expense for me whatsoever, yet there is great happiness in the hereafter;
whereas through hatred, there is the suffering of displeasure and great suffering in the next world.
One should speak with words that place the feet [of the composition] confidently, whose meaning is clear,
which are delightful, pleasant to the ear, rooted in compassion, and uttered in a soft and gentle tone.
One should always look upon sentient beings with an upright gaze, as if drinking them in with one's eyes;
by relying solely upon these, my Buddhahood shall come to be.

Merit arising from constant application and from firm resolve, as well as that arising from the cultivation of remedies, is great when directed toward fields of benefit and service, or toward those who suffer.
One should always be endowed with diligence and act for oneself;
one must not grant any opportunity to others in any of one's tasks.
The perfections, beginning with generosity, become increasingly superior;
one should not abandon a superior [virtue] for the sake of another, except in the case of the bridge of proper conduct.
Having understood this, one should always be intent upon the welfare of others;
for a compassionate person who perceives the true benefit, even that which is prohibited is permitted.
Having shared with those who have fallen into miserable states, the helpless, and those established in vows,
one should eat a moderate amount and cast away the three robes beyond [one's person].
One should not afflict this body, which serves the True Dharma, for the sake of other ends;
for in this very way, one shall swiftly fulfill the hopes of sentient beings.
Therefore, one should not give up one's life while the compassionate disposition remains impure;
however, when that disposition has become equal [to all beings], it may be sacrificed, for in this way one does not fall away.
One should not speak of the Dharma to one who lacks respect, who is in a state of physical ease, or whose head is wrapped;
nor to one who holds a parasol, a staff, or a weapon, or whose head is covered by a veil.
One should not show profound and noble [teachings] to those who are limited, nor to women in the absence of a man;
one should practice equal reverence toward both inferior and superior dharmas.
One should not enjoin a recipient of the vast Dharma to a base teaching,
nor should one, having abandoned proper conduct, entice others with sūtras and mantras.
The discarding of tooth-sticks and saliva is not permitted; it is undesirable in water or on ground fit for use, and the voiding of urine and such is likewise censured.
One should not eat with the mouth full, nor with noise, nor with the mouth wide open; one should not sit with legs dangling, nor rub the arms together.
One should not share a vehicle, a bed, or a seat with another's wife.
Having seen or heard anything that causes lack of confidence among people, one should avoid it all.
One should not point at anything with a single finger, but rather respectfully with the entire right hand; one should indicate even the path in this manner and so forth.
One should not call out to anyone with an uplifted arm even in a minor emergency;
rather, one should snap one's fingers or use a similar signal, otherwise one would be lacking in restraint.
One should lie down in the direction one desires, like the Teacher at the time of his parinirvāṇa,
remaining fully conscious, with the intention of rising quickly, and necessarily before [the end of the watch].
The conduct of Bodhisattvas has been described as immeasurable;
for now, one should certainly practice that conduct which purifies the mind.
Day and night, one should practice the Threefold Heap at the three times of the day;
by that, through reliance on the Bodhicitta and the Victors, all remaining downfalls are pacified.
Whatever states one may encounter, whether by one's own volition or under the power of others,
one should diligently train in those very precepts appropriate for each of those states.
For there is nothing whatsoever that is not to be learned by the sons of the Conquerors;
nor is there any merit that does not accrue to one who dwells in such a manner.
Whether indirectly or directly, one should perform no action other than for the sake of sentient beings;
and for the sake of sentient beings alone, one should dedicate everything toward enlightenment.
One should never abandon a spiritual friend, even for the sake of one's life—
such a friend who upholds the bodhisattva vow and is skilled in the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
One should learn how to attend upon a guru from the *Śrīsaṃbhavavimokṣa*;
this and other such matters taught by the Buddha are to be understood from reading the *sūtras*.
The trainings are seen in the sūtras; therefore, one should recite the sūtras.
Furthermore, one should examine the root downfalls in the Ākāśagarbha Sūtra.
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* must certainly be consulted again and again, because correct conduct is demonstrated therein in detail. (SBca 5.105)
Alternatively, one should briefly examine, with diligent effort, the *Sūtrasamuccaya* composed by the noble Nāgārjuna, and the second [work] as well.
Whatever one is restrained from, wherever, and for whatever reason—
one should observe and practice that training for the sake of protecting the minds of worldly beings.
This, in brief, is the definition of clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*):
that which is the repeated examination of the state of one’s body and mind.
I shall practice with my body alone; what would be the use of verbal recitation?
What will happen to a sick person by the mere recitation of a medical treatise?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Guarding Vigilant Awareness," in the *Pañjikā* on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
Chapter Six: The Perfection of Patience All this virtuous conduct, generosity, and worship of the Sugatas performed throughout thousands of eons—anger destroys it all. (SBca 6.1)
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore, one should cultivate patience with effort through various methods.
When the thorn of hatred remains in the heart, the mind finds no tranquility; it does not enjoy joy or happiness, nor does it attain sleep or steadfastness.
Even those who rely upon him and honor him with wealth and respect desire to kill that master, for he is ill-favored by their hatred.
Even friends are agitated by him; he gives nothing and is not served.
In short, there is nothing at all by which an angry person remains well-situated.
He who, perceiving anger as an enemy, destroys it through persistent effort because it produces such sufferings as these, shall be happy both in this world and in the next.
Born from the occurrence of the undesired and the obstruction of the desired,
hatred— having obtained its food in the form of mental distress— proudly destroys me.
Therefore, I shall deprive that enemy of his food;
for this foe has no task remaining other than my own destruction.
Even through the arrival of the most undesirable circumstances, my joy must not be disturbed;
for even in the presence of mental distress, there is nothing desirable gained, whereas virtue is diminished.
If there is indeed a remedy, what is the use of mental distress in that case?
But if there is no remedy, what is the use of mental distress in that case?
Suffering, humiliation, harshness, and ill repute are undesirable;
these same things are the opposite for one's beloveds, for oneself, and even for an enemy.
Happiness is obtained only with great difficulty, while suffering remains effortlessly present;
and liberation comes through suffering alone. Therefore, O mind, be firm!
The Durgāputrakas and Karṇāṭas endure in vain the pain of burning, cutting, and so forth for the sake of liberation; why then am I a coward?
There is no object whatsoever that is difficult for habituation to accomplish;
therefore, by practicing with mild pain, even great pain can be endured.
Do you not see the pointlessness of the sensations of gadflies, mosquitoes, and hunger and thirst, as well as the great suffering of itching and other such ailments?
One should not cultivate delicacy toward cold, heat, rain, wind, travel, disease, imprisonment, or beatings; otherwise, suffering will increase.
Some display great valor upon seeing their own blood, while others fall into a swoon even upon seeing the blood of another. (SBca 6.17)
Because that [mind] has arrived with both firmness and timidity,
one should therefore become difficult for suffering to conquer and should overcome affliction.
Even in the face of suffering, the wise person should not disturb the clarity of the mind;
for there is indeed battle with the afflictions, and pain is easily encountered in combat.
Those who, receiving blows from the enemy upon their own chests, conquer their foes—they are the victorious heroes; all others are merely slayers of the dead.
Furthermore, there is another virtue of suffering: through it, one sheds intoxication by means of spiritual urgency;
one develops compassion for those in cyclic existence, fear of evil, and a longing for the Victor.
I feel no anger toward bile and the other humors, even though they cause great suffering;
why then should I be angry with sentient beings? For they too are provoked by conditions.
Just as this pain arises even though it is not desired,
so too does anger arise by force, even though it is not desired.
A person does not become angry by intending "I shall be angry," nor does anger arise with the prior thought "It will arise. It arises spontaneously by its own impulse.
Whatever offenses and various evils there may be, all of that arises through the power of conditions; it does not exist independently.
The collection of conditions has no intention, "I shall produce";
nor does that which has been produced have the intention, "I have been produced. (SBca 6.26)
Whatever is indeed cherished as primary and imagined to be the self—
that very thing arises without being intentionally willed, out of the fear of existence.
For that which has not yet arisen does not exist; who then would desire to come into being?
And because it is occupied with its objects, it does not even strive to cease.
For the self is eternal, insentient, and clearly inactive like space;
even when in contact with other conditions, what action can there be for that which is changeless?
As before, what has been done by that [agent] at the time of the action?
In the relationship "this is his action," what is the basis for that connection?
Thus, everything is under the control of another, and that [controller] too is powerless;
since all things are thus motionless like magical illusions, where is there any cause for anger?
If it is argued that such prevention is not logical— asking "who prevents what?"—
it is indeed logical, because the cessation of suffering is held to depend upon conditions.
Therefore, whether one sees an enemy or a friend acting unjustly, one should be happy by reflecting: "Such are the conditions for this person."
If, however, accomplishment were achieved by one's own will alone for all embodied beings,
no one would experience suffering, for no one desires suffering.
Through negligence, they harm themselves with thorns and the like;
through anger, by depriving themselves of food and so forth; and through the desire to obtain women and other such things that are difficult to attain.
Some kill themselves by hanging or by falling from heights, by consuming poison or unwholesome food, and by the failure to practice virtuous conduct.
Since they thus destroy even their own dear selves by being under the power of the afflictions, how could there be any restraint toward the bodies of others?
When these beings, maddened by the afflictions, proceed toward their own destruction,
how can it be that not only is there no compassion, but rather anger arises?
If it is the very nature of fools to cause harm to others,
then anger toward them is not appropriate for me, just as it is not toward fire, whose nature is to burn.
Now, even if this fault were adventitious and beings were naturally gentle,
nevertheless, their anger would still be improper, like pungent smoke in the sky.
If, setting aside the primary agent such as the wielder of the staff, one becomes angry with the instigator,
then since that instigator too was impelled by hatred, it would be better for me to direct my hatred toward that hatred itself.
In the past, I too inflicted such very same suffering upon sentient beings;
therefore, it is entirely fitting for me, who caused such affliction to beings, to experience this.
That weapon and my body—both are causes of suffering.
Since I have taken up the weapon for the sake of the body, at what should I be angry?
This boil, shaped like a statue, has been grasped by me, blinded by craving; it is incapable of being touched—so when there is pain therein, at what should I be angry?
"I do not desire suffering, yet I, a fool, desire the cause of suffering; since suffering comes about through my own transgressions, why do I become angry with another? (SBca 6.45)
Just as the forest of sword-leaves and the birds of hell are produced solely by my own karma, so too is this; at whom, then, should one be angry?
Impelled by my own karma, they have become my wrongdoers;
since they will go to the hells, have they not indeed been slain by me alone?
Relying on these, my many sins are exhausted through my forbearance;
yet, by relying on me, they go to hells of long-lasting suffering.
"I alone am the wrongdoer toward these people, yet they are my benefactors;
why, having inverted this fact, do you, with a wicked mind, become angry? (SBca 6.49)
If my own intention were virtuous, and I did not go to the hells,
what would that have to do with them if I had merely protected myself?
Even if I were to retaliate against them, they would still not be protected;
furthermore, my own spiritual practice would decline, and thus those poor wretches would be lost.
Because it is formless, the mind cannot be slain by anyone anywhere;
yet, due to its attachment to the body, the consciousness is afflicted by suffering.
Insult, harsh speech, and infamy—this collection of things does not afflict the body; therefore, why does your mind become agitated?
If others have a lack of faith toward me, how could that consume me in this life or in another, such that it would be undesirable to me?
If he is undesirable to me because he creates an obstacle to my gain,
then my gain will perish right here, but my sin will certainly remain.
It would be better for me to die this very day than to live a false life for a long time;
for even if I were to remain for a long duration, that same suffering of death would eventually be mine.

One who awakens after experiencing happiness for a hundred years in a dream, and another who awakens after being happy for but a moment— [between these two, there is no difference in the duration of their actual experience].
Surely, happiness ceases for both once they have awakened;
that same analogy applies at the time of death to one who has lived long and one who has lived but a short while.
Even after obtaining many gains and enjoying pleasures for a long time,
I shall depart empty-handed and naked, like one who has been robbed.
If, while living for the sake of gain, I bring about the destruction of evil and the increase of merit,
surely for one who becomes angry for the sake of gain, there will be the destruction of merit and the increase of evil.
If that very purpose for which I live should perish,
what is the use of that life which accomplishes nothing but evil?
If you say that hatred toward one who speaks ill of others destroys sentient beings,
why does such anger not arise in you toward one who brings disgrace upon another?

Because lack of faith depends on another, you should be patient with those who lack faith; but one should not be patient with one who speaks ill out of affliction, for that depends on both the speaker and the listener.
Even toward those who destroy images, stupas, and the true Dharma, or who revile them, it is not fitting for me to feel hatred; for there is no suffering for the Buddhas and the rest.
Seeing that resentment arises toward those who harm one's beloved ones— such as teachers, paternal relatives, and so forth— one should restrain anger, just as described previously.
The suffering of embodied beings is invariably caused by both sentient and insentient factors;
since that suffering is seen to reside in the sentient being, therefore, forgive this suffering.
Some commit offenses out of delusion, while others, being utterly bewildered, become angry;
whom among these actions do we call faultless, or whom do we call the offender?
Why was this done previously, by which you are thus oppressed by others?
All are dependent upon their own karma; who am I here to act otherwise?
Having understood this, I shall likewise exert effort toward meritorious deeds,
so that all may come to possess minds of mutual loving-kindness.
Just as when a house is burning, the fire, having moved into another house, might become attached to straw and such; it is then dragged out and removed.
When the mind is thus scorched by the fire of hatred due to attachment,
it must be abandoned at that very moment, for fear of the total incineration of one's merit.
If one destined for execution is released after having his hand cut off, what is wrong with that?
If one is released from the hells by means of human sufferings, what is wrong with that?
If even this much suffering cannot be endured today,
why is anger— which is the cause of the torments of hell— not restrained?
For the sake of anger alone, I have been made to undergo this very same thing in hells thousands of times;
yet neither my own welfare nor the welfare of others has been accomplished by me.
And this suffering is not of such a kind that it will fail to accomplish a great purpose;
therefore, for one who removes the suffering of the world, joy in suffering itself is appropriate here.
If others have attained joy and happiness by praising one endowed with exalted virtues,
why, O mind, do you not likewise rejoice when praising him?
And this joy and happiness of yours is blameless and gives rise to bliss;
it is not forbidden by the virtuous, for it is the supreme means of winning over others.
If this [happiness] of yours were not dear to you as being "your own happiness," then by ceasing to give wages and so forth, your benefit in both the seen and the unseen worlds would be destroyed.
When your own virtues are being praised, you desire even the happiness of others;
yet when the virtues of others are being praised, you do not desire even your own happiness.
Having generated the mind of awakening out of a desire for the happiness of all sentient beings,
why do you now become angry with those very beings who have themselves obtained happiness?
It is said that you desire for sentient beings the state of Buddhahood, which is worthy of worship by the three worlds;
yet, seeing their fleeting honor, why do you burn with envy?
He who nourishes those whom you ought to nourish gives it to you alone;
having obtained one who sustains your family, you do not rejoice, but rather become angry.

How can you not desire the awakening of those beings for whose sake you yourself desire awakening? From where could the thought of awakening arise in one who becomes angry at the prosperity of others?
If that [gift] was not obtained by him because it remained in the house of the donor, in any case it does not belong to you; what is the use of that which has been given and then not taken?
What can merits do to prevent it? Or what can one's own pure virtues do? If, while obtaining them, you do not accept them, tell me: why are you not angry?
Not only do you fail to grieve for yourself for the evil you have committed,
but you even desire to compete with others who have performed meritorious deeds.
If something unpleasant has arisen for the enemy, what more could there be for your satisfaction? And it will not be without cause, occurring merely through your wish.
If that suffering were established by your own will, what pleasure could there be for you?
Or if it were indeed a benefit, what misfortune could possibly be greater than this?
For this is a terrible hook cast by the fisherman of the afflictions;
because the guardians of hell, having purchased you with it, will roast you in the cauldrons.
Praise, fame, and honor lead neither to merit nor to long life;
they are of no use for strength, nor for health, nor even for the physical pleasure of my body.
This much indeed would be the self-interest of a wise person who understands their own welfare:
that one desiring mental happiness should indulge in intoxicants, gambling, and the like.
For the sake of fame, they squander their wealth and even bring about their own destruction.
Are syllables something to be eaten? And once dead, whose is that pleasure?
Just as a child cries out in distress when a house of sand collapses,
so does my own mind appear to me when praise and fame are lost.
Since sound is devoid of mind, it is impossible for it to praise me;
rather, the fact that another person is pleased with me is indeed the cause of my joy.
What indeed is the use of affection for another directed toward me?
That pleasure of affection belongs to him alone; I have not even the slightest share in it.
If my happiness consists in being happy through the happiness of others, then let that happiness be mine everywhere;
why then do I not feel happy when others are made happy by the favor of someone else?
Therefore, the thought "I have been praised" gives rise to joy within oneself;
yet even in that case, because there is no such connection [between the self and the praise], it is merely the behavior of a child.
These things—praise and the like—destroy my peace and spiritual urgency;
they breed envy toward those with virtues and provoke anger at prosperity.
Therefore, those who have appeared before me to destroy my reputation and so forth are,
in fact, engaged in protecting me from falling into the lower realms.
For me, who seeks liberation, attachment to gain and honor is improper;
how could I feel hatred toward those who release me from bondage?
How can I feel hatred toward those who have become like door-bolts for one desiring to enter [the state] beyond suffering— as if by the very empowerment of the Buddha?
It is not fitting to feel anger toward one who has created an obstacle to merit;
for there is no austerity equal to patience—is this not now the very opportunity for it?
Now, if I do not practice patience here because of my own faults,
I have created this obstacle myself when the cause for merit has presented itself.
For that which does not exist without another, and which exists when that other is present—that alone is its cause; how can it be called an obstacle?
For a supplicant who arrives at the proper time does not create an obstacle to giving,
nor is it said that an obstacle to renunciation is created when a renunciant has arrived.
Beggars are easy to find in this world, but those who do harm are rare;
for no one offends me, even though I am without fault.
Therefore, an enemy who has been acquired through my own efforts is like a treasure discovered in one's own home; because he assists me in the practice of awakening, he is to be desired by me.
This fruit of patience has been acquired both by me and by him;
therefore, this should first be given to him, since patience was initiated toward him first.
If an enemy is not to be honored because he lacks the intention to achieve perfection through patience,
then how can the True Dharma be honored, even though it is devoid of consciousness, yet is the cause of perfection?
If an enemy, who possesses the intention to cause harm, is not honored, how can I possess patience toward one who exerts himself for my benefit like a physician?
Therefore, patience arises precisely by depending upon that very evil intention;
for this reason, that very person is the cause of my patience and should be honored by me like the True Dharma.
Therefore, the Sage has declared that the field of sentient beings is the field of the Victors,
for by propitiating these [beings], many have reached the further shore of prosperity.
Since the attainment of the Buddha-qualities is equal from both sentient beings and the Victors,
what is the logic in having such reverence for the Victors but not for sentient beings?
And the greatness of the intention is not inherent, but rather arises from its effects;
since that greatness is equal [in all], sentient beings are therefore equal by virtue of it.
That one is worthy of worship because of an intention of loving-kindness is simply the greatness of sentient beings;
that merit which arises from faith in the Buddha is simply the greatness of the Buddha.
Insofar as they have received a portion of the Buddha's teachings, sentient beings are equal to the Victors;
however, no one is equal to the Buddhas in their infinite qualities, which are like oceans.
If even a minute quality of those who are the sole mass of the essence of virtues is seen anywhere, even the three worlds would not be sufficient for its worship.
However, a portion of the source of the Buddha-dharmas exists within sentient beings;
by acting in accordance with this portion, one performs worship of sentient beings.
Furthermore, for those who are sincere friends and immeasurable benefactors,
what other recompense could there be than the act of pleasing sentient beings?
"For whose sake they break their own bodies and enter the Avīci hell, for them a deed done there would be a deed well done.
Therefore, even toward those who do great harm, one should practice only what is entirely beneficial."
Since even my own masters— for whose sake they are indifferent even to themselves—
how can I not show them honor as their servants, rather than treating them with pride?

Those in whose happiness the Lords of Sages find joy, and in whose suffering they enter into grief—by pleasing them, all the Lords of Sages are pleased; by harming them, an injury is done to the Sages.
Just as one whose body is ablaze on all sides finds no joy even through all sensual desires,
likewise for those whose nature is compassion, there is no means of finding pleasure even when sentient beings are suffering.
Therefore, whatever suffering I have caused to those who possess great compassion by bringing grief to living beings, I now confess that sin; may those sages forgive me for having troubled them.
Today, for the sake of propitiating the Tathāgatas, I enter into servitude in this world with my whole being;
let the multitudes of people place their feet upon my head or trample me, so that the Lord of the World may be pleased.
This entire world has been made their own by those whose very nature is compassion; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, these very beings are seen in the form of sentient creatures; they are the Lords themselves—how can there be any disregard for them?
This alone is the propitiation of the Tathāgatas; this alone is the accomplishment of one's own welfare;
this alone is the remover of the world's suffering; therefore, let this alone be my vow.
Just as a single king’s officer may harass a great multitude,
yet that far-sighted multitude is unable to retaliate against him.
Since he is not alone, for his strength is the king's army,
he would not thus humiliate any weak person who has committed an offense.
Since both the guardians of hell and compassionate beings derive their power from that [sentient being],
one should therefore serve sentient beings just as a servant serves a fierce king.
What could an angry king do that would cause the suffering of hell,
which is indeed experienced as a result of causing distress to a sentient being?
What could a pleased king give that would be equal to Buddhahood—
that which is experienced through bringing joy to sentient beings?
Let alone the future Buddhahood arising from pleasing sentient beings;
do you not see even in this very life the excellence of good fortune, fame, and stability?
Transmigrating through the realms of existence, the patient person attains a pleasing appearance, health, joy, long life, and the abundant happiness of a universal monarch.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Perfection of Patience," in the *Pañjikā* on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.

Chapter Seven: The Perfection of Vigor One who is thus patient should cultivate vigor, for awakening is established upon vigor; indeed, without vigor there is no merit, just as there is no movement without wind. (SBca 7.1)
What is vigor? It is enthusiasm for the wholesome. What is said to be its opposite?
Laziness, attachment to what is contemptible, despondency, and self-contempt. (SBca 7.2)
Through a craving for reliance on sleep, which is the savoring of the pleasure of non-activity,
and due to a lack of revulsion toward the sufferings of saṃsāra, laziness arises.
Scented by the hunter that is the afflictions, you have entered the snare of birth;
even now, do you not realize that you have come into the very mouth of death?
Even as your own companions are being slaughtered one by one, you do not see it;
nevertheless, you still fall asleep like a buffalo belonging to a Caṇḍāla.
For one who is being watched by the Lord of Death and whose path is blocked on all sides, how can eating be agreeable to you? How sleep? How pleasure?
Death will soon arrive once its provisions have been fully gathered;
even if you cast off that laziness now, what will you do when it is no longer time?
"This has not yet been attained; this has been begun; this remains half-finished"—while thinking thus, "Alas, I am destroyed! Death has arrived suddenly," [one suffers]. (SBca 7.8)
Beholding his kinsmen, their faces red with tears swollen by the force of grief and devoid of hope, as well as the faces of the messengers of Yama.
Tormented by the memory of your own sins, hearing the cries of the denizens of hell,
and with your limbs smeared by shrieks of terror, what will you do, overwhelmed as you are?
"It is only fitting for you to feel fear here and now, like a living fish;
how much more so for one who has committed evil, facing the intense sufferings of hell? (SBca 7.11)
O delicate one, you are tormented even by being touched with warm water;
having committed the karma of a hell-being, why do you remain so at ease?
Exerting no effort yet desiring results, so delicate and subject to much suffering, you are seized by death while appearing immortal; alas, O miserable one, you are being destroyed!
Having obtained this human vessel, cross over the great river of suffering;
O fool, this time for sleep has come, for such a boat will be difficult to find again.
Having abandoned the supreme delight in the Dharma, which is followed by an uninterrupted succession of joys,
how can you find pleasure in agitation, laughter, and the like, which are causes of suffering?
The absence of despondency, the power of the array of forces, the state of being subject to self-mastery,
the equality of self and others, and indeed the exchange of self and others.
One should not give way to despondency by thinking, "How can there be awakening for me?
because the Tathāgata, who speaks the truth, has declared this to be true.
They were also gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, and worms,
by whom the supreme enlightenment so difficult to attain was reached through the power of their resolve.
How much more so, then, can I—a human by birth—discern what is beneficial and what is harmful?
By not abandoning the principles of the Omniscient One, why should I not attain enlightenment?
Furthermore, I have this fear that I might have to give away my hands, feet, and so forth;
such confusion regarding what is weighty and what is light would be mine through a lack of discernment.
I must be cut, split, burned, and even torn apart many times over for incalculable millions of eons, yet awakening will still not be attained.
But this suffering of mine, which is limited, is for the sake of accomplishing perfect enlightenment;
it is like the pain of having a splinter extracted once that splinter's agony has been removed.
All physicians bring about health through the hardships of medical treatment;
therefore, to destroy many sufferings, one must endure a small amount.
Even this appropriate treatment the excellent physician did not administer;
for he treats those who are gravely ill with sweet and gentle care.
At first, the Leader even enjoins one to the giving of vegetables and the like;
later, through that sequence, he causes one to do that which one would eventually give away even one's own flesh.
When wisdom arises toward one's own flesh as it does toward vegetables,
then for one who abandons both flesh and bone, what indeed is difficult to do?
He is not suffering because he has abandoned evil, nor is he dejected because of his wisdom;
for it is through false conceptualization in the mind that suffering arises in the body from evil.
Through merit the body is happy, and through wisdom the mind is happy;
remaining in cyclic existence for the sake of others, by what means could the compassionate one be weary?
Exhausting former misdeeds and receiving oceans of merit,
one proceeds even more swiftly than the Śrāvakas solely through the power of the thought of awakening.
Thus, proceeding from happiness to happiness, what conscious person would despair,
having obtained the chariot of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), which removes all weariness and fatigue?
The power of aspiration, abiding, delight, and liberation is for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings;
one should generate aspiration out of fear of suffering, while contemplating the benefits.
Having thus uprooted the opposing factors, one should strive to increase enthusiasm by means of the powers of zeal, self-confidence, delight, renunciation, dedication, and mastery.
I must destroy the immeasurable faults of both myself and others—
faults for which even oceans of eons would not suffice to bring about the exhaustion of even a single one.
In that regard, not even a trace of my effort toward the destruction of faults is seen;
how is it that my chest does not burst asunder while I am made to endure immeasurable agony?
Many virtues are to be acquired by me for both myself and others;
the cultivation of even a single one of those virtues might not be accomplished even in aeons as vast as oceans.
I have never cultivated even a fraction of virtue;
my wondrous birth, obtained with such difficulty, has been spent in vain. (SBca 7.36)
I have not attained the happiness of the great festival of worshipping the Blessed One; I have performed no service for the Teaching, nor have I fulfilled the hopes of the poor.
I have not granted safety to those who were afraid, nor have I brought happiness to those who were distressed;
I have only become a thorn in my mother's womb for her sole suffering.
Due to my previous lack of zeal for the Dharma, such a misfortune has now befallen me; who then would ever abandon zeal for the Dharma?
