The Sage declared that the root of all wholesome qualities is aspiration;
the root of that, in turn, is the constant cultivation of the fruit of maturation.
Sufferings, mental distresses, various fears,
and the frustration of desires arise for those who commit evil deeds.
Wherever the aspiration of those who perform virtuous deeds may go,
there it is honored by the value of its fruits through their merits.
But wherever one who commits evil goes in pursuit of happiness,
there and then he is struck by the weapons of suffering born of those very evils.
Seated within the centers of vast, fragrant, and cool lotuses,
their splendor nourished by the food of the sweet voice of the Jina,
their noble forms emerge from the lotuses awakened by the hand of the Sage.
Through their wholesome deeds, they become sons of the Sugata in the presence of the Sugata.
His entire complexion stripped away by the messengers of Yama, crying out in agony, his body drenched as if poured with molten copper from the heat of fire,
and the flesh of his limbs hacked away by hundreds of blows from flaming swords and spears—
Due to his many unwholesome deeds, he falls repeatedly upon the ground of intensely heated iron.
Therefore, having cultivated a virtuous aspiration with such care,
one should practice self-respect by means of the ritual prescribed for Vajradhvaja.
Having first examined the necessary conditions, one should either begin or not begin;
indeed, it is better not to begin at all than to turn back after having begun.
That habit persists even in other births, and suffering increases due to evil; furthermore, the time for action has passed, and that goal remains unaccomplished.
Pride should be understood as threefold, pertaining to actions, secondary afflictions, and capacities. The thought, "I alone must perform this," is pride regarding action.
This world is independent of its afflictions and is incapable of accomplishing its own welfare;
therefore, I must act on their behalf, for I am not like other people who are powerless.
Another person performs base actions while I am still present;
if it is out of pride that I do not do this, then let my pride perish—it is better for me that it should.
Having encountered even a dead lizard, even a crow acts like Garuḍa;
so too, even a slight misfortune afflicts my mind if it is weak.
Indeed, misfortunes are easily overcome by one who is rendered motionless by despondency;
but one who has risen up and exerts effort is difficult to conquer even for the great.
Therefore, with a firm mind, I shall overcome adversity with adversity; for one who has succumbed to adversity, the desire to conquer the three worlds becomes a mere joke.
For everything must be conquered by me; I am not to be conquered by anyone.
This pride must be borne by me, for I am the son of the Lion of the Victors.
Those beings who have conquered pride are the best; they are not arrogant.
An arrogant person falls under the power of the enemy, and such are those who are under the sway of the enemy that is pride.
Led to miserable rebirths by pride, even when born as humans they are deprived of joy;
subsisting on the alms of others, they are slaves, fools, ill-favored, and emaciated.
Even those ascetics who are despised by all and stiff with pride—
if they too are among the proud, tell me, what kind of people are the miserable?
Those alone are truly proud and victorious, those alone are heroes who carry pride for the sake of conquering the enemy that is pride;
they who, having struck down that enemy of pride even while it is surging, bestow upon people at will the fruit of victory.
Though he may stand amidst thousands of arrogant ones belonging to the side of affliction,
he remains far removed from the hosts of defilements, like a lion among a herd of deer.
For even in great hardships, the eye does not perceive taste;
likewise, even when encountering difficulty, one should not fall under the power of the afflictions.
Whatever action one falls into, one becomes addicted to that action;
intoxicated by that action and insatiable in soul, like one who desires the pleasure of the fruits of play.
Action is performed for the sake of happiness, yet happiness may or may not result;
but for one to whom action itself is happiness, how can he be happy when free from action?
There is no satisfaction with sensual desires in cyclic existence, which are like honey on a razor’s edge;
how then could there be satisfaction with the nectar of merit, which is auspicious and sweet in its maturation?
Therefore, even at the conclusion of one's actions, one should immerse oneself in that very practice,
just as an elephant, scorched by the midday sun, plunges first into a lake it has reached.
If, however, there is a consequence of the loss of strength, one should abandon the undertaking;
and once it is well completed, one should let go of it through a desire for what comes next.
One should protect against the blows of the afflictions and strike firmly at the afflictions themselves,
like one engaged in a sword-fight with a skilled enemy.
Just as one who is afraid would swiftly seize a sword that has fallen, so too should one,
mindful of the hells, swiftly seize the sword of mindfulness when it has slipped away.
Just as poison spreads through the body upon reaching the blood,
so too does a fault spread within the mind upon finding a vulnerability.
Just as one carrying a vessel of oil, guarded by men with swords in their hands,
would be intent on avoiding a stumble out of fear of death, so too should the practitioner of the vow be.
Therefore, just as one springs up quickly when a snake has fallen into one's lap,
so too should one act with haste when sleep or laziness approach.
Having thoroughly repented for each single transgression, one should reflect:
"How can I act so that this shall not happen to me again? (SBca 7.72)
For this reason, one should seek association or action so that the practice of mindfulness may indeed occur during those various states. (SBca 7.73)
One should thus make oneself light by recollecting discourses on heedfulness,
so that one remains ready in every situation, just as before, regarding the arrival of tasks.
Just as cotton is subject to the coming and going of the wind, so too should one come under the power of enthusiasm; in this way, supernatural power (ṛddhi) is perfected.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Perfection of Vigor," in the *Pañjikā* on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
Chapter Eight: The Perfection of Meditative Concentration (Dhyānapāramitā) Having thus increased one's enthusiasm, one should settle the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
For a person whose mind is distracted stands between the fangs of the afflictions (*kleśa*). (8.1)
Through physical and mental seclusion, distraction cannot arise;
therefore, having abandoned the world, one should avoid discursive thoughts.
The world is not abandoned because of affection, nor through craving for gain and the like;
therefore, in order to renounce these, the wise person should reflect in this way: SBca_8.3.

Realizing that one who is well-joined with insight through calm abiding effects the destruction of the afflictions, one should first seek calm abiding; and that is attained through a delight that is indifferent to the world.
For whom could there be affection for things that are impermanent,
when one will not see a beloved person again for thousands of lifetimes?
Not seeing [the truth], one falls into discontent and does not abide in meditative concentration;
even upon seeing it, one is not satisfied, and as before, one is tormented by thirst.
He does not see things as they truly are; through his agitation he falls away, and he is consumed by that grief and his longing for union with what is dear.
Through constant preoccupation with that [worldly life], one's brief lifespan passes away in vain again and again;
by means of this impermanent phenomenon, the eternal Dharma is lost.
One who associates with fools will certainly go to an evil rebirth;
one who does not desire such dissimilar association—what can be gained from the company of fools?
In one moment they become friends, and in a moment they become enemies;
ordinary people are difficult to satisfy and prone to anger even when there is cause for joy.
When spoken to for their own benefit, they become angry and restrain me from what is wholesome;
yet if their words are not heeded, they fall into miserable states when provoked.

Envy arises from one who is superior; rivalry from one who is equal; pride from one who is inferior; intoxication from praise; and resentment from blame—when, then, could any benefit ever come from a fool?
Self-exaltation, disparagement of others, talk of delighting in cyclic existence— such things,
and whatever else is unwholesome, inevitably belong to the fool by virtue of his foolishness.
Thus, for him as well, through association with that [world], there is the occurrence of misfortune;
therefore, I shall dwell alone, happy and with an unafflicted mind.
One should flee far from the foolish; when encountering them, one should propitiate them with pleasant words.
However, one should not engage in continuous intimacy, but rather remain like a neutral, virtuous person.
Taking only the essence of the Dharma as a bee takes honey from flowers,
I shall wander everywhere like a stranger, unacquainted with anyone.
"I am successful, I am honored, and many desire me"—
from the realization that such a mortal must face death, fear arises.
Wherever the mind, deluded by pleasure, finds delight,
there that very thing arises and remains as a thousandfold suffering.
Therefore, the wise person should not desire that [suffering], for from desire fear is born; this [suffering] passes away of its own accord, so one should remain patient and wait.
Many became gainful and many became famous;
yet, along with their gains and fame, they were not known where they had gone.
Others despise me; why should I rejoice when praised? Others praise me; why should I despair when reviled? (SBca 8.21)
Sentient beings with diverse inclinations have not been satisfied even by the Victors;
how much less so by ignorant ones like me? Therefore, what is the use of worrying about the world?
They revile the being who gains nothing and they find fault with the one who gains;
how can delight arise for them in such companionship that is by nature painful?
The Tathāgatas have stated that a fool is not the friend of anyone;
for no joy arises in a fool except for his own self-interest.
The joy that arises through the gateway of one's own self-interest is merely joy for the sake of the self;
for it is like the agitation felt at the loss of wealth, since that agitation is caused by the loss of pleasure.
Trees do not harbor resentment, nor must they be propitiated with effort;
when shall I dwell together with those who are so pleasant to live with?
Staying in an empty temple, at the foot of a tree, or in caves,
when will I go forth without concern, never looking back?
When shall I dwell in vast regions that are by nature unowned, my abode for wandering at will?
Possessing only a clay bowl as my wealth and robes that thieves cannot enjoy,
when shall I dwell without fear, no longer protecting this body?
When shall I go to my own natural place, the ground of the body, and compare my own body— subject to the law of decay— with other skeletons?
For this very body of mine will become so putrid that even jackals would not approach its vicinity because of the stench.
Even for this single body, the fragments of bone that are born together will go their separate ways; how much more so, then, for other beloved people?
A single being is born, and indeed a single being dies;
no one else shares in that suffering. So what is the use of dear ones who act as obstacles?
Just as one who has set out on a journey takes up residence in various dwellings along the way,
so too does the traveler of existence take up residence in successive births.
Before he is led away by four men,
and while he is still being mourned by the world, one should go to the forest at that very moment.
Through non-attachment and non-opposition, one who is alone in body,
having already died to the world, does not grieve when actually dying.
And no one moving nearby, even if grieving, causes him distress;
nor do any distract him from his recollection of the Buddha and the other [objects of mindfulness].
Therefore, solitude— delightful, effortless, the source of auspiciousness,
and the pacifier of all distractions— should always be cultivated by me.
Freed from all other thoughts, with a mind one-pointedly focused on my own heart,
I shall strive for the concentration and the taming of the mind.
For sensual desires produce misfortune both in this world and in the next;
in this world through bondage, execution, and mutilation, and in the next through rebirth in the hells and other such realms.

For whose sake you have many times joined your palms in supplication to male and female messengers, and for whose sake you previously disregarded sin and ill repute; [for that very purpose, you must now act].
I have cast myself into danger and squandered my wealth;
yet, it was by embracing these very things that I attained the highest bliss.
Why do you not attain peace by embracing at will those very same bones— none other than your own, now under your control and free from possessiveness?
Whether previously seen or unseen, her face was once covered by a veil, being raised up with effort or lowered down out of modesty.
Behold, its face has now been revealed by the vultures as if they could no longer endure your suffering; why do you flee now?
That which was protected even from the falling glances of others has now been devoured; O envious one, why do you not protect it today?
Seeing this heap of flesh being devoured by vultures and other scavengers,
[one realizes that] for others it is honored as food with garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments.
You feel terror even at this motionless skeleton when it is thus beheld;
why then do you not feel fear when it is being moved by some vetāla?
From a single morsel of food, both saliva and impurity arise for these beings;
since you find that impurity undesirable, how can the drinking of saliva be pleasing to you?
Those possessed by desire do not take pleasure in soft pillows filled with cotton, thinking, "It does not leak a foul odor," for they are deluded by impurity.
If this passion exists even when concealed, why would that which is unconcealed be undesirable?
If there is no purpose in it, why is the concealed part being crushed?
If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another—
a cage of bones bound together by sinews and smeared with the mud of flesh?
Your own body is full of much impurity; maintain your resolve with that very thing. O consumer of excrement, forget this other bag of filth.
"You desire to see and touch it, thinking, 'I am fond of its flesh';
how can you desire that which is by nature insentient flesh?"
That mind which you desire to see cannot be seen or touched; and that which can be touched and seen, you do not know it to be the mind—so why do you embrace it in vain?
It is not surprising that you do not perceive another’s body as consisting of impurity;
it is a wonder that you do not recognize your own body as being likewise composed of impurity.
Having abandoned the young lotus, which blossoms at the rays of the cloudless sun, what pleasure can there be for a mind intoxicated by impurity within this cage of excrement?
If you do not wish to touch clay or other impure substances because they are smeared with filth,
then how can you wish to touch that which has issued from your own body?
If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another?
That seed was produced from a field of filth and has been nurtured by it.
Because it is small and born of impurity, you do not desire an unclean worm;
yet you desire this body, which is composed of much impurity and born from impurity.
O consumer of excrement, you not only fail to feel disgust for your own impurity,
but you even desire the vessels of others' filth.

Even the ground is considered impure when it has come into contact with pleasing things such as camphor and the like, or with rice and condiments that have been cast away after being placed in the mouth.
If you do not even resolve that this [body] is impure despite it being directly perceived,
then look at other terrifying bodies fallen in the charnel ground as well.
Since great fear arises when the skin is torn away,
how can one, knowing this, again find pleasure in that very same thing?
Even though this fragrance is applied to the body, it comes from sandalwood alone and from nothing else;
why then do you take delight in one thing because of the fragrance belonging to another?
If passion does not exist here because of the natural foulness [of the body], then surely there is no auspiciousness; why does the world, delighting in what is useless, smear it with perfume?
What does this have to do with the body here, even if the sandalwood is fragrant?
Why should one be attached to one thing because of the fragrance belonging to another?
If the body— with long hair and nails, with teeth stained yellowish-white by grime, covered in filth and mud, naked, and naturally terrifying— [is thus], [then why do you not feel revulsion?]
Why is it being refined with such effort, like a weapon for self-destruction?
The earth is overrun by madmen intent on deluding themselves.
Indeed, you feel revulsion upon seeing a few skeletons in a cemetery;
yet you take delight in a village-cemetery, which is crowded with moving skeletons.
And thus, even this impurity cannot be obtained without a price;
for its sake, there is the toil of acquisition and the suffering in the hells and other realms.
A child lacks the capacity for acquisition; by what means could he be happy in youth?
Youth passes away through acquisition; once old, what can one do with desires?
Some, exhausted by their activities at the end of the day, being addicted to base pleasures,
return home in the evening and lie down as if they were dead.
Others, distressed by the hardships of travel during military expeditions,
do not see their wives and children even after many years, as they are intent on that very purpose.
That very purpose for which the self was sold by those deluded by desire has not been attained; instead, life has been spent in vain through the labor of others.
The wives of those who have sold themselves into servitude and are constantly engaged in menial tasks give birth to others in forest thickets and similar places.
Indeed, deluded and mocked by desire, they enter into battle where life is in doubt merely to live; for the sake of honor, they go into servitude.
Some who are full of desire are being cut; others are seen impaled on stakes, being burned, and struck by spears.

Know that wealth brings endless misfortune through the sorrows of acquiring, protecting, and losing it; for those whose minds are attached to riches and who are thus distracted, there is no opportunity for liberation from the suffering of existence.
Thus, for those possessed by desire, the disadvantage is great while the gratification is small,
just like the seizing of a mouthful of fodder by a beast of burden pulling a cart.
For the sake of that mere fragment of taste, which is not difficult even for a beast to obtain,
this extremely rare perfection of a moment has been destroyed by one cursed by fate.

This exertion which has been made at all times for the sake of this body— which is inevitably destined to perish, is insignificant, and leads to falls into hell and other lower realms— [is utterly futile].
Therefore, even with a hundredth part of the effort required for Buddhahood, one might attain it;
yet the suffering of the practices is far greater than that, and such enlightenment is not for those possessed by desire.
Neither weapons, nor poison, nor fire, nor falling into an abyss,
nor enemies can serve as a comparison for sensual desires, when one recalls the agonies of hell and other such realms.
Thus, having become weary of sensual desires, one should generate delight in solitude— in the peaceful forest lands that are free from strife and fatigue.
On fortunate days, upon delightful stone slabs as vast as palace terraces and cooled by the sandalwood-like rays of the moon,
fanned by the silent and gentle forest breezes, they walk to and fro and contemplate the welfare of others.
Having dwelt for as long as desired in empty houses, at the foot of trees, or in caves,
he wanders at will, free from the weariness of protecting possessions and detached from expectations.
Dwelling wherever he pleases and dependent on no one,
the happiness of contentment that he enjoys is difficult even for Indra to attain.
By cultivating the qualities of solitude through such modes as these,
one should, with discursive thoughts stilled, cultivate the spirit of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
First, one should cultivate equanimity toward oneself and others with such earnestness:
"All beings, being equal in their desire for happiness and aversion to suffering, must be protected by me just as I am."

Just as this body, though manifold through its various parts such as the hands and so forth, must be protected as one, so too is this entire world; though diverse, it is of the same nature in its suffering and happiness.
Even though my own suffering does not afflict other bodies,
nevertheless, that very suffering is unbearable to me because of my attachment to self.
Likewise, even if another's suffering is not perceived by me through my own self, nevertheless,
that suffering of theirs is unbearable to me because of my attachment to the self.
I must destroy the suffering of others because it is suffering, just like my own suffering;
I must also benefit others because they are sentient beings, just like myself.
Since happiness is equally dear to me and to others, what is so special about myself that I should strive for my own happiness alone?
When fear and suffering are not dear to me or to others,
then what is the distinction of my own self, that I should protect it and not another?
If it is not protected on the grounds that "I am not afflicted by its suffering," then why protect against the suffering of my future body, since that too does not afflict me now?
The notion that "I am that very same person even then" is a false conceptualization,
because it is one who has died and quite another who is born.

If it is held that whatever suffering belongs to a person must be protected by that very person, then why is the pain of the foot not protected by the hand? For the pain of the foot does not belong to the hand.
Even if this [unwholesome action] proceeds from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*),
that which is improper must be turned away— both one's own and that of others— to the best of one's ability.
The continuum and the collection are false, like a row or an army;
since he who possesses suffering does not exist, to whom will that [suffering] belong?
All sufferings whatsoever are without an owner; because they are suffering, they must be warded off without distinction. What basis is there for such restriction?

If it is asked why suffering should be prevented, [the answer is] because there is no dispute among anyone that it should be so; and if it should be prevented, then all [suffering] should be prevented in this same way, for one's own self is just like other sentient beings.
If compassion produces much suffering, why does it arise with such force?
Having examined the suffering of the world, how could this suffering born of compassion be considered great?
If the suffering of many can be dispelled by the suffering of one,
then that suffering ought to be intentionally produced by one who is compassionate toward both self and others.
Therefore, although Supuṣpacandra knew of the danger from the king,
he did not eliminate his own suffering for the sake of removing the suffering of many others.
Thus, those whose mental continuums have been cultivated in this way, for whom the suffering of others is as dear as their own joy,
plunge into the Avīci hell like swans entering a lotus grove.
When sentient beings are being liberated, there arise oceans of joy;
surely that alone is sufficient—what need is there for a liberation devoid of flavor?
Therefore, even after performing deeds for the sake of others, there should be neither pride nor astonishment;
nor should there be a longing for the fruit of maturation, due to an exclusive thirst for the welfare of others.
Therefore, just as I protect myself even from the slightest disparagement,
I shall likewise cultivate a mind of protection and a mind of compassion toward others.
Through habituation, the cognition "I" arises even with respect to drops of semen and blood belonging to another, even though the object is unreal.
Likewise, why is another's body not grasped as the self?
For one's own body to be regarded as "other" is already established and is by no means difficult.
Having recognized oneself as being full of faults and others as oceans of virtues,
one should cultivate the relinquishing of one's own selfhood and the taking up of others.
Just as hands and other limbs are accepted as parts of the body,
why are embodied beings not likewise accepted as parts of the world?

Just as the notion of a self arises through habituation toward this body of ours which is devoid of self, why should the sense of selfhood not likewise arise toward others through habituation? (SBca 8.115)
Thus, even after performing the welfare of others, there is neither pride nor astonishment; and just as when one has fed oneself, no expectation for a reward arises.
Therefore, just as you wish to protect yourself from pain, grief, and the like,
so too should you practice a mind of protection and a mind of compassion toward the world.
Therefore, the Protector Avalokita bestowed his own name [upon the Bodhisattva] in order to remove even the fear of timidity before an assembly for the sake of people.
One should not turn back from difficult tasks because of the power of habituation;
for that very thing which causes terror upon hearing of it, by that same thing one finds delight.
He who wishes to quickly protect both himself and others should practice the supreme secret: the exchange of self and other.
Since one feels fear even at the slightest danger due to excessive attachment to this self, who would not hate that self? For the destruction of the enemy brings fear.
He who kills birds, fish, and deer out of a desire to remedy his own weakness, hunger, thirst, and so forth, and who stands as an obstacle on the path; SBca 8.122.
One who, for the sake of gain and honor, would even kill his own parents or seize the property of the Three Jewels, thereby becomes fuel for the Avīci hell.
What wise person would desire, protect, or honor such a self?
One should not look upon him as an enemy, nor should anyone treat him with contempt.
"If I give, what shall I eat?"—this is the state of a *piśāca* for one's own sake; "If I eat, what shall I give?"—this is the state of a king of gods for the sake of others. (SBca 8.125)
Having oppressed another for one's own sake, one is cooked in the hells and other realms of misery;
but by oppressing oneself for the sake of others, all forms of excellence are attained.
By transferring that very desire for one's own exaltation— which leads to miserable rebirths, low status, and folly— onto another, one attains a happy rebirth, honor, and wisdom.
By commanding another for one's own sake, one experiences servitude and the like;
but by commanding that same person for the sake of another, one experiences lordship and the like.
Whoever in the world is suffering, all do so out of a desire for their own happiness;
whoever in the world is happy, all do so out of a desire for the happiness of others.
What is the use of saying more? Behold this difference between the fool who seeks his own interest and the sage who acts for the sake of others.

Indeed, Buddhahood is not something to be accomplished; how then could there be happiness even in cyclic existence for one who does not effect an exchange of their own happiness for the suffering of others? (SBca 8.131)
Let alone the next world; even an object perceived in this life is not accomplished when a servant does not perform his work or when a master does not pay his wages.
Abandoning the production of mutual happiness and the festival of joy both seen and unseen,
deluded beings grasp at terrible suffering born from inflicting pain upon one another.
Whatever calamities arise in the world, and however many sufferings and fears there may be—all these result from grasping at a self; so why do I grasp at this [body]?
Without abandoning the self, suffering cannot be abandoned;
just as without abandoning fire, burning cannot be abandoned.
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying my own suffering and for the sake of pacifying the suffering of others,
I give myself away to others and take others as myself.
O mind, form the firm resolve: "I am bound to others. Having relinquished the welfare of all sentient beings, you must not think of anything else now.
It is not proper for the eyes and other faculties belonging to another to perceive their own objects;
nor is it proper for hands and other limbs belonging to another to exert themselves for one's own sake.
Therefore, being devoted to sentient beings, whatever you perceive within this body,
eliminate each and every one of those things and act for the benefit of others.
Having conceived of yourself as being among those who are inferior and others as being yourself,
you should cultivate envy and pride with a mind free from conceptual construction.
"This person is honored, not I; he is a recipient of gain, not I;
he is praised as I am censured; I am suffering, while he is happy. (SBca 8.141)
"I perform actions, but he remains well-established;
he is indeed great in the world, while I am indeed lowly and devoid of merit. (SBca 8.142)
What can be done by one who is devoid of virtues, for the Self of everyone is endowed with virtues?
There are those among whom I am base, and there are those among whom I am excellent.
I am to be treated by the power of the afflictions, such as the failure of ethical discipline and right view, and not by my own will;
I have accepted even this suffering according to my capacity.
Furthermore, since I am incurable for him, why do you despise me?
What use have I for these virtues; he alone is the one possessed of virtue.
While still within the jaws of the beast of miserable rebirths, his compassion for living beings is such that he seeks to surpass even the wise by means of his superior qualities.
Since one should regard oneself as equal [to others] in order to increase one's own excellence,
one may even achieve gain and honor for oneself through quarreling.
May my virtues become manifest everywhere in the world;
yet, may there be some of his virtues that no one at all shall ever hear.
"May my faults be concealed; may I receive honor, while he receives none.
Today I have gained great profit, for I am honored while he is not. (Bodhicaryāvatāra 8.149)
We shall see him, after a long time, made a fool of— laughed at by all the people and reviled here and there— and we shall rejoice.
For even this wretched fellow indeed competes with me;
yet what learning does he have? What wisdom, beauty, lineage, or wealth?
Having thus heard my own virtues being proclaimed here and there,
with my hair standing on end and my heart filled with joy, I shall enjoy a festival of happiness.
Even if he should obtain some gain, we should take it from him by force,
provided that by giving him merely enough for his sustenance, he performs our work.
This one must be made to fall from happiness and always be joined with our own suffering;
by means of him, we shall all be made to experience the sufferings of cyclic existence hundreds of times over.
Immeasurable eons have passed while you have sought to know your own self-interest;
through this great exertion, you have acquired nothing but suffering.
At my request, act here in this manner without hesitation;
you shall see these benefits later, for the word of the Sage is indeed true.
If you had previously performed this action,
then— apart from the bliss of the Buddha’s perfection— this present state would not have occurred.
Therefore, just as you have conceived an ego-sense toward the drops of semen and blood belonging to others, so too should you cultivate that same sense toward other things.
Becoming a spy for others, whatever you perceive within this body,
take that very thing away for their sake and act for the benefit of others.
"This one is well-off while that one is miserable; this one is lowly while that one is high;
that one does something while this one does not"—do not harbor such envy within yourself.
Deprive yourself of happiness and subject yourself to the suffering of others;
examine his deceit (or fruit), asking: "What is he doing, and when? (SBca 8.161)
Cast even a fault committed by another upon his very head;
and reveal even the slightest fault of this great sage.
Defile his reputation with talk of the superior fame of others;
and make him carry out tasks for living beings like a lowly slave.
For this person is composed of faults and is not to be praised for any adventitious qualities;
therefore, act in such a way that no one may perceive his virtue.
In brief, whatever harm you have done to others for your own sake,
cast that same suffering upon yourself for the sake of sentient beings.
One should not give him any encouragement that would make him talkative;
rather, he should be established in the conduct of a new bride—modest, fearful, and restrained.
"Do this; remain thus; this must not be done by you.
In this very way you must be brought under control, and restrained if you transgress. (SBca 8.167)
Even when it is being told this, if you, O mind, will not do so, I shall surely subdue you alone; for all faults are dependent upon you.
"Where will you go, now that you have been seen by me? I shall destroy all your pride! That was another time in the past when you were able to destroy me."
Abandon now the hope that "I still have my own self-interest";
you have been sold by me to others, so do not think of much suffering.
If, out of negligence, I do not give you away among sentient beings,
you will undoubtedly deliver me to the guardians of hell.
Thus, having been made to suffer for a long time by you through various such acts,
I shall now slay you, a servant of your own self-interest, calling to mind those ancient enmities.
If you have affection for yourself, you should not take pleasure in [harming] others;
if this self must be protected, it is not proper that it be protected [in such a way].
Just as this body is provided with protection,
it becomes increasingly more delicate, yet in that very same way it falls apart.
Even when he has fallen into such a state, this entire earth is not sufficient to satisfy his desire; who then will fulfill his wish?
For one who desires the impossible, suffering and the frustration of hope arise;
but for one who is free from hope in all things, prosperity never decays.
Therefore, one should not grant the body any scope for the increase of its desires;
for that object which is not grasped because of its desirability is what is truly called "auspicious."
This body, which ends in a state of ashes, is motionless and moved by another;
it is a terrible vessel of impurity—why then do I have such attachment to it?
What use have I for this machine, whether living or dead? What difference is there between it and a clod of earth? Alas! Why do you not let go of this egoism?
Through partiality toward the body, suffering is acquired in vain;
for what is the use of hatred or affection toward this thing that is like a piece of wood?
Whether it has been protected by me or devoured by vultures and other scavengers, there is neither affection nor aversion toward it; why then do I feel attachment?
If he whom I provoke to anger feels no resentment, and he whom I honor feels no joy— if he does not even know [my intent], for whose sake then is my exertion?
Those who desire this body are indeed said to be my friends;
since everyone desires their own body, why are they not dear to me?
Therefore, disregarding my own interests, I have renounced my body for the welfare of the world;
thus, even though it is full of many defects, it is maintained like a vessel of karma.
Therefore, enough with the conduct of the world; remembering the discourse on heedfulness and warding off sloth and torpor, I shall follow the wise.
Therefore, in order to destroy the obscurations, I shall practice meditative concentration,
drawing the mind away from the wrong path and making it continuous with its own object of focus.
The eighth chapter, titled "The Perfection of Meditation," from the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Wisdom.
For the Sage taught this entire collection of requisites for the sake of wisdom;
therefore, one should generate wisdom out of a desire for the cessation of suffering. (SBca 9.1)
The conventional and the ultimate—these are considered the two truths.
Reality is that which is beyond the scope of the intellect; the intellect is said to be the conventional.
In this regard, the world is seen to be twofold: the yogi and likewise the ordinary person.
Among them, the ordinary world is sublated by the world of the yogi.
Even yogins are surpassed by those who follow after them through their superior intellectual distinctions;
this is seen by both parties as a matter of common experience for the sake of practical action, provided one does not engage in analytical investigation.
Phenomena are perceived by the world and also conceptualized as being real;
however, there is no dispute between yogis and the world regarding the fact that they are like an illusion.
Even that which is perceived, such as form and so forth, is not established by way of valid cognition;
like the common consensus of purity regarding what is impure, it is false.
And for the sake of leading people into the world, entities were taught by the Protector;
in reality they are momentary, yet if [this is so], it does not contradict conventional truth.

There is no fault for those who perceive reality, when acting according to the conventional truth of yogis, as distinguished from that of the world; otherwise, there would be contradiction with worldly consensus in the case of describing a woman as impure.
How can there be merit from a Victor who is like an illusion, even if he exists in reality?
If a sentient being is like an illusion, how can he be born again after dying?
As long as the collection of conditions exists, so long does illusion persist;
how can a sentient being exist in reality merely through a long continuity?
In cases such as the killing of an illusory person, there is no sin because of the absence of a mind;
however, when the mind and illusion are both present, there arises the production of both sin and merit.
Because mantras and the like lack such power, the mind of illusion does not arise from them;
for that illusion, too, being of various kinds, arises from various conditions,
and no single condition possesses the capacity for everything anywhere.

If one who is extinguished in the ultimate sense were to wander in cyclic existence conventionally, then even a Buddha would likewise wander; what, then, would be the use of the practice for enlightenment?
If conditions are not severed, even illusion is certainly not severed;
however, through the severance of conditions, there is no possibility of existence even conventionally.
But when there is a severance of conditions, even conventionally it does not arise;
since even delusion no longer exists, by what is the illusion perceived?
When even illusion itself does not exist for you, then what is perceived?
Even if that form belongs to the mind alone, it does not exist as something other [than the mind] in reality.
When the mind itself is an illusion, then what is seen by whom?
And it has been said by the Lord of the World: "The mind does not see the mind."
Just as the edge of a sword does not cut itself, so too the mind [does not harm itself];
and just as a lamp illuminates its own form, so it is with the mind—if this is your argument.
A lamp is not illuminated at all because it is not enveloped by darkness;
for a crystal that is blue is not dependent on anything else for its blueness, just as a blue object is not.
Likewise, some things are seen to depend on others, while others are independent;
for instance, that which is not blue cannot be blue, just as a cause of blue is observed.
For if it is already blue, who could make itself blue by itself?
If it were not blue, it could not make itself blue by itself.
Having known that "the lamp shines," it is spoken by means of cognition;
but having known that "the intellect shines," by whom is this spoken?
Whether manifest or unmanifest, when it is not perceived by anyone,
it is as futile as describing the playful dance of the daughter of a barren woman.
If self-awareness does not exist, how can consciousness be remembered?
Memory arises from a connection with what was experienced by another, just like the poison of a rat.
Because it is seen when conjoined with other conditions, the lamp illuminates itself;
yet a jar seen through the application of a magical ointment does not become that ointment.
What is seen, heard, and known is not at all denied here;
rather, it is the conceptualization [of these] as real that is to be prevented, for it is the cause of suffering.

If it is conceived that illusion is neither other than the mind nor non-other, [then consider: if it were a real entity, how could it be neither other nor non-other? If it is not so, it does not exist as a real entity.
Just as an illusion is seen even though it does not exist, so too is the mind the seer.
If saṃsāra were based on a real entity, it would be otherwise, like space.
How could non-existence possess activity by depending on a real entity?
For, according to you, the mind would then become solitary, lacking any companion.
When the mind is freed from the grasped object, then all are Tathāgatas.
And what benefit is gained by even imagining "mind-only"?
Even when things are known to be like an illusion, how is affliction removed?
For even the creator of an illusory woman may still give rise to passion for her. (SBca 9.31)
For the latencies of the afflictions regarding the objects of knowledge have not been abandoned by its creator;
therefore, at the time of that [false] view, his latency for emptiness is weak. (SBca 9.32)
Through the cultivation of the impression of emptiness, the impression of existence is abandoned;
and by practicing the thought that "nothing exists," even that [impression of emptiness] is later relinquished.
When no entity is found which could be conceptualized as "non-existent," then how could a non-entity, being without a basis, stand before the mind?
When neither existence nor non-existence presents itself before the mind, then,
due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes objectless and is stilled.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-granting tree fulfill one's desires,
so too is the form of the Victor perceived through the power of those to be trained and his own prior aspirations.
Just as a snake-charmer, having empowered a ritual pillar, passes away;
even long after he has perished, that pillar continues to neutralize poisons and the like.
In accordance with his conduct toward enlightenment, even the pillar of the Victor accomplishes all tasks, even when the Bodhisattva has passed into nirvāṇa.
How can an offering made to one who is without mind be fruitful?
For it is taught that [the merit] is exactly the same whether [the Buddha] is present or has entered parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, how is it that an offering made to a true Buddha is fruitful, whether according to scripture, or conventionally, or even in reality? Just as [it is said]: "In that regard, the fruit arises from scripture, whether conventionally or in truth; an offering made to a true Buddha is fruitful. (SBca 9.40)
Liberation comes from seeing the truth; what is the use of seeing emptiness?
For it is stated in the scriptures that there is no awakening without this path.
Now, the Mahāyāna is unestablished; how then is your scripture established?
Since that [scripture] is established for both [parties], it was not established for you from the very beginning.
Whatever basis for trust you have in that [Veda], place it likewise in the Mahāyāna;
otherwise, if truth were desired by both parties, then the Veda and other such texts would also possess truth.
If you claim that the Mahāyāna is subject to dispute, then abandon your own scripture as well,
for it is disputed by non-Buddhists, and other scriptures are disputed by both your own and others.
The teaching has monkhood as its root, yet even monkhood itself is difficult to maintain for those whose minds possess objective referents; even nirvāṇa is difficult to maintain for them.
If liberation results from the abandonment of the afflictions, let it occur immediately thereafter;
for the efficacy of karma is observed even in those who are free from afflictions.
If it is considered that craving does not constitute grasping, then is this craving of theirs not present even if it is non-afflicted, just as their delusion is? (SBca 9.47)
Craving has feeling as its condition, and these [beings] possess such feelings;
therefore, one should abide with a mind that has an object of focus, wherever that may be.
Without emptiness, the mind arises bound once again;
therefore, one should cultivate emptiness, as in the case of the attainment of non-perception.
If a statement is accepted as the word of the Buddha because it appears in a sūtra,
why do you not consider the Mahāyāna to be essentially equal to your own sūtras?
If everything were faulty because of one thing that is not accepted,
then why is everything spoken by the Victor not [accepted] simply because of one [point] that is equal to the Sūtras?
That which cannot be fathomed even by the foremost disciples headed by Mahākāśyapa—
who, because they have not realized the truth, would not accept it— whom else will take it up?
Through liberation from attachment and fear, stability is achieved within cyclic existence;
this is the fruit of emptiness for the sake of those suffering through delusion.
Thus, in this way, a refutation against the position of emptiness is not tenable;
therefore, emptiness must indeed be cultivated without any doubt.
For emptiness is the antidote to the darkness of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations;
how could one who desires swift omniscience not cultivate it?
Since fear arises from that thing which produces suffering,
and emptiness is the pacifier of suffering, why then does fear arise from it?
If there is fear from this or that because of something called "I," and if that "I" is indeed something real, then for whom will there be fear?
I am not the teeth, hair, or nails; I am not the bone, nor am I the blood; I am not the nasal mucus, nor the phlegm, nor the pus, nor even the lymph.
I am not the fat, nor the sweat, nor the marrow, nor the blood;
I am not the entrails or the nirguṇḍī plant, nor am I feces or urine.
I am not flesh, nor sinew, nor heat, nor am I wind;
I am not the cavities, nor in any way the six consciousnesses.
If that [cognition] were the cognition of sound, then sound would be perceived at all times;
but what does it know in the absence of an object of knowledge (jñeya), by virtue of which it is designated as "cognition"?
If that which is ignorant were knowledge, it would follow that a piece of wood is knowledge;
therefore, it is certain that there is no knowledge in the absence of an object of knowledge.
If it perceives that very form, why does it not hear [sound] as well?
If you say it is because of the absence of sound, then that cognition [of sound] would likewise be non-existent.
How can that which has the nature of perceiving sound be the perception of form?
A single entity is conceived as both father and son, but not in reality.
Since neither the son nor the father consists of sattva, rajas, or tamas,
one's own nature— which is characterized by the apprehension of sound— is not perceived as belonging to them.
If that very same thing appears in another form like an actor, it too is impermanent;
if it were to possess a different intrinsic nature while remaining the same, then this would be a novel kind of identity.
If that other form is unreal, let your own true nature be stated.
If it is said to be consciousness, then it follows that all persons are one.
When there is identity between the sentient and the insentient because their existence is equal,
and when their distinction is false, then what can be the basis for their similarity?
And I am certainly not insentient, because I lack sentience, like a cloth or similar objects.
If, on the other hand, I am a knower by virtue of being joined with consciousness, then it follows that when I am ignorant, I would be destroyed.
If the self remains entirely unmodified, what has consciousness done for it?
Thus, the selfhood of one who is ignorant and inactive is considered to be like that of space.
If the connection between action and its fruit is not tenable without a self,
then once the agent has perished after performing the action, to whom will the fruit belong?
Since the fruits of action are established as having distinct substrates for both of us,
and since the self is inactive therein, is not this debate indeed futile?
"It possesses a cause and is joined with a fruit"—this is not possible [in reality].
It is taught that there is an "agent" and an "experiencer" by relying on the unity of the continuum.
The mind of the past and the future is not "I," for that indeed does not exist.
If "I" am the mind that has arisen, then once this has perished, "I" no longer exist.
Just as the trunk of a plantain tree is nothing when divided into its parts,
so too am I non-existent when sought through analytical investigation.
If it is argued that if a sentient being does not exist, for whom would there be compassion? [The answer is:
It is for one who has been imagined through delusion by someone who has committed himself to the task for the sake of a purpose.
If there were no sentient being, for whom would there be anything to be done? Indeed, such striving arises from delusion;
however, the delusion regarding what ought to be done is not to be prevented when it aims at the cessation of suffering.
The ego-sense is the cause of suffering, yet it increases due to delusion regarding a self;
if it cannot be turned back even by that [realization], then the cultivation of selflessness is better.
The body is not the feet, nor the shanks, nor the thighs; the body is not the hips, nor the belly, nor the back, nor the chest, nor the arms.
There are no hands, nor these two sides, nor the armpits, nor the characteristics of the shoulders;
there is no neck, nor the head—then what, indeed, is the body here?
If this body exists in all [parts] by way of its parts,
then while the parts exist in their own parts, where does it itself reside?
If the body were present in its entirety in every part, such as the hands and so forth,
then there would be as many bodies as there are those hands and other parts.
The body exists neither within nor without; how, then, can it be in the hands and other limbs?
Since it does not exist apart from the hands and so forth, how indeed does it exist at all?

That body does not exist; rather, due to delusion, there is the cognition of a "body" with respect to the hands and so forth, just as there is the cognition of a "man" with respect to a tree stump because of a particular arrangement [of parts].
As long as the collection of conditions persists, so long does the body appear like a person;
likewise, as long as that collection exists in the hands and other limbs, so long is the body seen there.
In this way, because it is a collection of fingers, even the foot would be nothing;
that too, because it is a collection of joints, and even the joint, because of the division of its own parts.
Even parts are divided by atoms, and even that atom is divided according to its spatial directions;
since spatial division implies a lack of parts, there is no such thing as an atom, and therefore space is not composed of atoms.
Thus, what discerning person would feel attachment toward form, which is like a dream?
When even the body does not exist in this way, then who is a woman and who is a man?
If suffering exists in reality, why does it not afflict those who are intensely joyful?
And if things such as delicacies were truly pleasant, why would they not be pleasing to one afflicted by grief and the like?
If that [feeling] is not experienced because it is overwhelmed by something more powerful,
how can it be a feeling when its very nature is not experience?
Indeed, suffering exists in its subtle form; has its grossness not been removed?
If there were something else beyond mere contentment, then that too would be its subtlety.
If suffering does not arise when a contrary cognition occurs,
then has it not indeed followed that feeling is merely an adherence to conceptual construction?
For this very reason, this investigation is cultivated as its antidote;
for yogins have the food of meditative concentration produced from the field of conceptual construction.
If the sense faculty and its object are separated by an interval, how could there be contact between them?
Even if they were without an interval, how could they be one; what could possibly have conjunction with what?
One atom cannot enter another atom, for it is devoid of space and is equal [in size].
Without entry, there can be no mingling; and without mingling, there can be no conjunction.
And how indeed can conjunction be possible for that which is partless?
If you have seen conjunction in something partless, then demonstrate it.
However, for consciousness, which is formless, conjunction is not at all tenable;
nor is that of a collection, because it is unreal, as was previously analyzed.
Thus, in the absence of contact, how could there be the arising of sensation?
For what purpose is this exertion? To whom would there be affliction, and from what would it arise?
When there is no feeler whatsoever and feeling itself does not exist, then,
having seen this state, O craving, why do you not shatter?
It is seen and even touched by a mind whose nature is like a dream or an illusion;
because it arises simultaneously with that mind, feeling is not perceived as something separate.
That which has arisen previously and subsequently is remembered, not experienced;
it does not experience itself, nor is it experienced by another.
There is no experiencer whatsoever distinct from the sensation;
thus, in reality, in this selfless collection [of factors], who is it that is oppressed by this?
The mind does not abide in the sense faculties, nor in form and so forth, nor in between them;
neither within nor without, nor elsewhere is the mind to be found.
That which is neither in the body nor elsewhere, neither mixed nor separate anywhere—that is nothing at all; therefore, sentient beings are by nature in a state of final nirvāṇa.
If cognition exists prior to the object of knowledge, upon what basis could it arise?
If cognition exists simultaneously with the object of knowledge, upon what basis could it arise?
If, on the other hand, knowledge were to arise after the object of knowledge, then from what would that knowledge itself arise?
And thus, the arising of all phenomena cannot be established.
If that were so, and conventional reality did not exist, then from where would the two truths come?
Or, if it too existed through another conventionality, how could sentient beings ever attain liberation?
This is a conceptual construction of another's mind; however, it does not exist by way of its own conventional nature.
If that [conceptualization] is later determined to be non-existent, then conventional reality itself would not exist at all.
Conceptual construction and the conceptually constructed—these two are mutually dependent;
all investigation is said to proceed by relying upon what is conventionally established.
But when that very analysis is itself analyzed by another analysis,
then there is an infinite regress, because that analysis too must be subjected to further analysis.
But when the object of investigation has been investigated, there is no basis for further investigation;
because it lacks a basis, it does not arise, and that is called nirvāṇa.
But he for whom both of these are real is in an extremely precarious state:
if the object exists by virtue of the knowable, what then is the status of the existence of knowledge itself?
Now, if knowledge exists by virtue of the object of knowledge, what is the status of the existence of that object?
Or, if they exist by virtue of each other, then both would be non-existent.
If there is no father without a son, how can there be the birth of a son?
In the absence of a son, there is no father; thus, both of them are non-existent.
A sprout is born from a seed, and by that very [sprout] the seed is indicated;
why then is the existence of that [seed] not understood through the knowledge produced from the object of knowledge?
From the knowledge that the sprout exists, it is understood that the seed exists;
but from what is the existence of that knowledge itself known, by which the object of knowledge is apprehended?
In this world, everyone perceives through direct observation that everything depends upon a cause;
for indeed, the various distinctions among lotuses, stalks, and so forth arise from a distinction in their causes.
If it is asked what causes the distinction between causes, it is due to the differentiation of prior causes.
And if it is asked why a cause yields its fruit, it is through the power of prior causes.
The Lord is the cause of the world; tell me, first of all, who is this Lord?
If you say it is the elements, let it be so; what is the point of such exertion over a mere name?
Furthermore, earth and the other elements are manifold, impermanent, devoid of activity, and not deities; they are to be transgressed and are indeed impure—therefore, they are not that Lord.
Space is not the Lord because it is inactive; nor is the self, since that has been previously refuted.
Furthermore, how can it be said that the agency of the inconceivable is itself inconceivable?
What is it that he desires to create? If it is the self, then surely that is eternal;
likewise, the earth and other elements, the Lord, and primordial knowledge are all beginningless and dependent upon their objects of cognition.
Tell me, what has been created by that karma which results in pleasure and pain?
If there is no beginning to the cause, how could there be a beginning to the fruit?
Why does he not act at all times? For he does not depend on anything else;
since there is nothing else uncreated by him, what could he possibly depend upon?
If the cause depends upon a collection of conditions, then God does not;
for He is not able to act when the collection is absent, nor is He unable to act when it is present.
If the Lord acts without desire, he would be subject to another;
even if he acts with desire, he would be dependent on that desire. For one who acts in this way, how can there be lordship?
Those who assert that atoms are eternal have also been refuted previously.
The Sāṃkhyas, for their part, maintain that *pradhāna* is the eternal cause of the world.
The qualities known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, when existing in equilibrium, are called *pradhāna*; when they are in disequilibrium, they are said to be the world.
It is illogical for a single entity to possess three natures; therefore, that [nature] does not exist.
Likewise, qualities do not exist, for they too are each threefold.
Furthermore, in the absence of qualities, the existence of sound and so forth is utterly remote;
and since cloth and such things are insentient, pleasure and the like are impossible even there.
If you claim that entities have those [pleasures and so forth] as their cause, then surely entities have already been analyzed.
Furthermore, pleasure and the like are the causes, and from them cloth and such things do not arise.
Pleasure and the like would belong to the cloth and such; in the absence of those [objects], pleasure and the like do not exist.
Furthermore, the permanence of pleasure and the like is never perceived.
If the manifestation of pleasure truly exists, why is it not perceived?
That very same thing becomes subtle; how can it be both gross and subtle at once?
Having abandoned grossness, it becomes subtle; since grossness and subtlety are impermanent, why is impermanence not accepted for all things in that same way?
If grossness is not distinct from pleasure, then the impermanence of pleasure is evident.
If it is thought that nothing arises from non-existence because of its lack of being, [then how can pleasure arise from the non-existent state of grossness?]
The production of a manifest thing from what is non-existent is established for you even against your will;
if the fruit were already present in the cause, then one who eats food would be an eater of impurity.
One should buy cotton seeds with the very price intended for cloth and wear them;
if the world does not see this due to delusion, such is the situation even for one who knows the truth.
Furthermore, the world also possesses that knowledge; why then does it not see?
If you argue that the world is not an authority, then even clear perception would be non-existent.
If that which is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) were itself invalid (*apramāṇa*), then surely what is cognized by it would be false;
consequently, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of entities would not be established in reality.
Without contacting an imagined entity, its non-existence cannot be apprehended;
therefore, since the entity itself is false, its non-existence is clearly false as well.
Therefore, when a son is lost in a dream, the conceptualization that "he does not exist" obstructs the arising of the conceptualization of his existence; and that [conceptualization] is false.
Therefore, through such investigation, nothing exists as being without a cause,
nor is anything established within conditions, whether taken individually or collectively.
It has not come from anywhere else, nor does it stay, nor does it go;
what difference is there between this and an illusion, that it is treated as real by the deluded?
That which is created by illusion and that which is produced by causes—from where does it come, and to where does it go? Let this be investigated.
That which is seen through the proximity of another is not seen due to its own absence;
since it is artificial and like a reflection, how can there be any reality in it?
What purpose does a cause serve for an entity that already exists?
And if it does not exist, what purpose does a cause serve?
There is no transformation of a non-entity even by means of hundreds of millions of causes;
while it remains in that state, how could it become an entity, or what else has ever attained the nature of an entity?
If existence does not occur at the time of non-existence, when will existence ever come to be?
For that non-existence cannot be dispelled by an entity that has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, as long as non-existence has not departed, there is no possibility for existence to arise;
nor does existence ever attain the state of non-existence, for that would entail the consequence of having two natures.
Thus, there is neither cessation nor existence at any time;
therefore, this entire world is unborn and unceasing.
The realms of existence are like dreams when investigated; they are like plantain trees.
In reality, there is no distinction between those who have attained liberation and those who have not.
Thus, when all phenomena are empty, what could be gained and what could be lost?
Who could be honored or insulted, and who could come into being?
Whence comes pleasure or pain? What is dear and what is not dear?
What is craving, and where does that craving exist when sought by its very nature?
Upon reflection, who is this world of living beings? Who indeed here will die?
Who will come to be, who has been, who is a kinsman, and who is whose friend?
Let those like me regard everything as being like space;
they become angry and they rejoice due to the causes of quarrels and festivities.
Desiring happiness for themselves, those who commit evil deeds pass their time with great difficulty, beset by grief, exhaustion, despondency, and mutual cutting and piercing.
Having died, they fall into miserable states of long and intense suffering;
yet having come again and again to happy rebirths, they become accustomed to happiness.
In cyclic existence there are many precipices, and therein such unreality;
therein there is mutual contradiction, and therein no such reality exists.
And therein lie incomparable, intense, and endless oceans of suffering;
therein lies such feebleness of strength, and even therein, the brevity of life.
Even there, one is beset by the activities for livelihood and health, by hunger, fatigue,
and exhaustion, by sleep, by afflictions, and likewise by fruitless association with the foolish.
Life passes away quickly and in vain; therein, discernment is difficult to find.
Even if one possesses it, whence can there be the capacity to ward off the distractions one has long practiced?
Even there, Māra strives to cast one into the great abyss of the miserable realms;
furthermore, because of the abundance of false paths there, doubt is difficult to overcome.
Furthermore, the opportunity for a favorable moment is rare, the appearance of a Buddha is exceedingly difficult to encounter,
and the flood of afflictions is hard to ward off— alas, what a succession of sufferings!
Alas! How truly pitiable are these beings who dwell in a flood of suffering, yet do not perceive their own wretched state, even though they are so extremely ill-situated.
Just as someone who, having bathed again and again, might repeatedly enter the fire,
even so do those who are in extreme misery consider themselves to be in a state of well-being.
For those who sport as if they were ageless and immortal, wandering in this manner,
terrible calamities will arrive, having placed death right before them.
When shall I bring peace to those scorched by the fire of suffering,
using my own provisions for happiness produced from the clouds of merit?
When shall I teach emptiness to those who hold the view of apprehension,
through conventional non-apprehension, with devotion to the accumulation of merit?
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the Perfection of Wisdom, in the *Pañjikā* commentary on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
The Tenth Chapter: Dedication.
By whatever merit I have gained from reflecting upon this *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, may all beings be adorned with the practice of awakening.
May all those throughout every direction who are afflicted by physical and mental suffering obtain oceans of happiness and joy through my merits.
May there never be a loss of happiness for them as long as saṃsāra lasts;
may the world attain the uninterrupted bliss of a bodhisattva.
May all embodied beings in whatever hells exist throughout the world-systems rejoice with the bliss and joy of Sukhāvatī.
May those afflicted by cold obtain warmth, and may those afflicted by heat become cool,
through oceans of water produced from the great clouds of the Bodhisattvas.
May the Forest of Sword-Leaves for them have the splendor of the Nandana Grove,
and may the thorny Śālmali trees become wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees.

May the regions of hell become heart-pleasing through lakes whose beauty is delightful with the clamor of kadamba ducks, kāraṇḍava geese, ruddy sheldrakes, swans, and the like, and which are filled with the fragrance of abundant lotuses.
May that heap of coals become a heap of jewels, and may the scorched earth become a floor of crystal;
may the mountains of hellish conflagration become celestial palaces for worship, filled with Sugatas.
From this day forward, let there be a rain of flowers instead of the rain of burning coals, heated stones, and weapons;
and let that mutual battle with weapons henceforth be a flower-battle for the sake of sport.
May those whose flesh has fallen away, whose bodies are mere bones the color of jasmine, and who were submerged in the Vaitaraṇī river whose waters are like fire,
obtain divine forms through the power of my merit and dwell upon the Mandākinī together with celestial maidens.
Terrified, they suddenly behold here the messengers of Yama and the dreadful crows and vultures;
"Whose gentle sovereign is this, who produces happiness and joy, and by whom has the darkness been destroyed on all sides?"—
thus looking upward, they see Vajrapāṇi blazing in the expanse of the sky.
Having seen [them], may those whose misdeeds have been dispelled through the force of their joy go along with him.
A rain of lotuses, mixed with fragrant water, falls,
extinguishing the fires of hell with a "chham" sound;
as they behold this destruction, the hell-beings, suddenly gladdened by the thought, "What is this?", are granted the sight of the Lotus-handed One.
"Come, come quickly! O brothers, dispel our fear! We have been restored to life;
here has arrived for us some young Cīrī, who radiates blazing fearlessness. By his power alone, every calamity has vanished and surges of joy have arisen."
The mind of awakening that has arisen, and compassion, which is the mother who protects all beings.
Behold him, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the crowns of hundreds of gods,
whose gaze is moist with compassion, upon whose head falls a rain of many heaps of flowers,
and who is attended by thousands of celestial women singing praises amidst delightful gabled pavilions.
Upon seeing Mañjughoṣa before them, let there now be a great clamor from the denizens of hell!
Thus, may those in the hells rejoice upon beholding the clouds of bodhisattvas led by Samantabhadra— unobstructed by my own virtues— and the rains of cool, fragrant breezes that bring happiness.
May the intense sufferings and the fears of the hell-beings be stilled;
may all those dwelling in the miserable realms be liberated from those states of woe.
May the fear of devouring one another depart from the animals;
may the hungry ghosts become happy, like the humans in Uttarakuru.
May the *pretas* be fully satisfied and always bathed,
becoming cool by means of the streams of milk flowing from the hands of the noble Avalokiteśvara.
May the blind see forms, and may the deaf always hear;
may pregnant women give birth without pain, like Queen Māyā.
May they obtain clothing, food, drink, garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments—
everything their hearts desire that is conducive to their welfare.
May those who are afraid be fearless; may those afflicted by grief find joy;
and may those who are agitated become free from agitation and possessed of steadfastness.
May those who are sick attain health; may all be liberated from bondage;
may the weak become strong, and may they have affectionate hearts toward one another.
May all directions be auspicious for everyone traveling on the road;
may whatever purpose they go forth to be accomplished by the appropriate means.
And may those embarked upon sea voyages have their desires fulfilled;
having reached the shore in safety, may they rejoice together with their kinsmen.
May those who have strayed onto wrong paths in the wilderness find the company of a caravan,
and may they travel without fatigue, free from fear of robbers, tigers, and other dangers.

May the deities provide protection for those who are asleep, intoxicated, or distracted; for those in danger from disease, wild forests, and the like; and for the helpless, the young, and the elderly.
May they be forever liberated from all unfavorable conditions, endowed with faith, wisdom, and compassion,
perfected in their physical appearance and conduct, and always possessed of the memory of their past lives.
May they possess inexhaustible treasuries, as vast as the treasury of space;
may they be free from conflict and free from distress, living with self-reliant conduct.
May those beings who have little splendor possess great splendor;
may those ascetics who are deformed become endowed with perfect beauty.
May whatever women there are in the world attain manhood;
may those who are lowly attain high status, and may they be free from pride.
By this merit of mine, may all sentient beings without exception,
having desisted from all misdeeds, always perform what is wholesome.
Never separated from the mind of awakening, devoted solely to the conduct of awakening,
they are embraced by the Buddhas and remain free from the activities of Māra.
May all those sentient beings have immeasurable lifespans;
may they always live in happiness, and may even the very word "death" perish.
May all directions become delightful with groves of wish-fulfilling trees,
filled with Buddhas and their spiritual sons, and enchanting with the sounds of the Dharma.
May the ground everywhere be free from gravel and the like, level as the palm of a hand, soft, and made of lapis lazuli.
May the great assemblies of the Bodhisattvas' maṇḍalas sit down on all sides and adorn the surface of the earth with their own splendors.
Let the sound of the Dharma be heard without ceasing by all embodied beings— from the birds, from all the trees, from the rays of light, and even from the sky.
May they always attain union with the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas,
and may they worship the Teacher of the World with infinite clouds of offerings.
May the god send rain in due season, may there be an abundance of crops,
may the world be prosperous, and may the king be righteous.
May medicinal herbs be effective; may mantras be accomplished for those who recite them;
and may ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, and others be filled with compassion.
May no sentient being be suffering, nor sinful, nor diseased;
may none be inferior or despised, and may no one be dejected in mind.
May the monasteries be well-established, filled with the recitation and study of the scriptures; may there always be harmony within the Saṅgha, and may the work of the Saṅgha be accomplished.
May the monks who have attained discernment and desire the training meditate with pliant minds, free from all distractions.
May the bhikṣuṇīs be successful and free from quarrels and weariness; likewise, may all those who have gone forth possess unimpaired ethical discipline.
May those who are immoral become conscientious, always devoted to the destruction of evil;
may they attain a happy rebirth and there maintain their vows without violation.
May the wise be refined, may those who live on alms be successful,
may their mental continuums be pure, and may their fame be renowned in all directions.
Without experiencing the suffering of the miserable realms and without the practice of austerities,
may the world attain Buddhahood with a single divine body.
May all the perfectly awakened Buddhas be honored in manifold ways by all sentient beings;
may they be exceedingly happy with the inconceivable bliss of a Buddha.
May the aspirations of the Bodhisattvas for the sake of the world be fulfilled;
may whatever those Protectors intend for sentient beings come to fruition.
May the Pratyekabuddhas and likewise the Śrāvakas be happy,
being constantly honored with reverence by gods, asuras, and humans.
Through the protection of Mañjughoṣa, may I always attain the recollection of past lives and the state of renunciation, until I reach the Stage of Joy.
May I sustain myself with whatever seat is available, endowed with strength,
and may I obtain the necessary conditions for dwelling in solitude throughout all my births.
And whenever I should desire to see him or wish to ask anything,
may I behold that very Lord, Mañjunātha, without any obstacle.
In accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings throughout the expanse of the ten directions,
may my conduct be exactly as that of Mañjuśrī.
As long as space endures,
and as long as the world endures, may I remain, destroying the sufferings of the world.
Whatever suffering there is in the world, may it all ripen upon me;
and by all the virtues of the Bodhisattvas, may the world be made happy.
May the Teaching— the sole medicine for the suffering of the world, the source of all prosperity and happiness— endure for a long time, accompanied by gain and honor.
I pay homage to Mañjughoṣa, by whose grace my mind is directed toward what is auspicious;
I revere the spiritual friend, by whose grace [this wisdom] increases.
The tenth chapter of the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: Dedication.
This *Bodhicaryāvatāra* is completed;
it is the work of the master Śāntideva.
